You are executing the `analysis-sut` skill's study (its step 6 subagent). Follow its method exactly as written below. This is a CALL from another skill (review-ci-system), not a human reader — so return the WHOLE payload: every field, every diagram, the contradictions. Hold nothing back, make no offer, do not compress to two lines.

TARGET: /home/jack/src/testcase-validator  (absolute). FOCUS: none — the whole system.

METHOD — steps 1 to 5, in this order:

Step 1. Read the ground truth FIRST. The real artifacts, in whatever form this project has them: entry points, the build/package manifest, the schema, route definitions, container/compose files, config and its defaults, the top-level layout. Trace how the parts CONNECT, not just what they are. Comments inside source count as code and are read here. Where ground truth lives varies — the question is always "what does this actually run".

Step 2. Find #1 BEFORE listing anything. #1 is the organizing idea: what this is, why it exists, how its parts form one whole. For a multi-part system that is usually how components compose and depend on each other; for a single tool, the core abstraction or main flow. Find it before enumerating features — a feature list assembled first will not add up to an idea afterwards. Then #2 onward, each grounded in #1. Rank them.

Step 3. About three key points. FOUR AT MOST. Shorten by shortening — never by dropping a diagram from a key point that stays, and NEVER by folding one key point into #1. #1 states the organizing idea and carries no other key point's mechanism.
Prefer a BEHAVIOUR to a DESCRIPTION. "Rules are rows read once at startup" describes structure and yields a row nothing can ever fill; "three refusals, one per stage — schema, rules, the call itself" names something a test either covers or does not. This list is what test coverage will be measured against, so every key point must be phrased as something a test could cover.

Step 4. Settle the list, THEN draw. Before drawing anything ask: is any behaviour explained only inside another key point's mechanism? A yes means it is a key point — promote it, and take step 3's route out of the cap (demote the weakest, or go to five and say why the list is five). Ask again over the new list until the answer is no. Only then count.
Then draw one ASCII diagram per key point, #1 included. Draw the REAL mechanism with REAL names from the code — boxes labelled "service" and "database" describe every system ever built and this one not at all. Keep every diagram inside 80 columns. COUNT CHECK: diagrams drawn == key points on the settled list.

Step 5. ONLY NOW read the prose files — README, architecture records, example config, anything under a docs directory — and only to report where they CONTRADICT the code: a table that does not exist, a command that would fail, a route never defined, a described mechanism that was replaced. This pass belongs to you, the one who read the code; do not hand it back. Report every contradiction found, or "none found".

RETURN, for each key point, all seven fields:
  # (rank, #1 is the organizing idea) | Key point (one concrete line) | Ground truth (the absolute paths it was derived from) | Mechanism (what actually happens, in the CODE'S OWN NAMES: real functions, routes, tables, types) | Why it matters (what a newcomer cannot understand without it) | Diagram (ASCII, one per key point) | Contradicts (any doc claim the code does not support, or "none")

CONSTRAINTS — these bind you absolutely, and your result MUST state explicitly which of them you held:
1. YOU WRITE NO FILE ANYWHERE. Not in the target repo, not in this repo, not in a scratch or temp directory, not a cache. No Write, no Edit, no NotebookEdit, no shell redirection (`>`, `>>`, `tee`), no `mkdir`, no `touch`. The list is returned in your reply and lives in the session only.
2. DO NOT MODIFY /home/jack/src/testcase-validator IN ANY WAY. Read only. No git commands that change state.
3. THE DOCS STAY SHUT UNTIL STEP 5. Do not open README.md, CONTEXT.md, CLAUDE.md, or anything under docs/ until you have derived the model from code. Reading them first supplies a model and everything after gets read as confirmation of it.
4. DO NOT RUN THE PROJECT'S TEST SUITE. Do not run npm test / npx / vitest / jest or any test command.
5. DO NOT START OR STOP ANY CONTAINER. No docker, no docker compose, no podman — not even `ps`/`up`/`down`.
6. DO NOT DERIVE KEY POINTS FROM TEST FILES OR TEST NAMES. The test suite is the thing under examination elsewhere; deriving the standard from the subject makes any suite look complete. You may note that a test directory exists, but do not read test files to decide what the system must do.
7. Do not read any issue, design document, draft, session log, or any other skill file. Your sources are the target repo's code, config and (at step 5 only) its own prose files.

Also report the count check result (diagrams == key points) and your answer to the absorption question from step 4.

- codebase-memory: Use the codebase knowledge graph for structural code queries. Triggers on: explore the codebase, understand the architecture, what functions exist, show me the structure, who calls this function, what does X call, trace the call chain, find callers of, show dependencies, impact analysis, dead code, unused functions, high fan-out, refactor candidates, code quality audit, graph query syntax, Cypher query examples, edge types, how to use search_graph.
- karpathy-guidelines: Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring code to avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria.
- agent-workflows:do-task: Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
judges whether it finished. - Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for
choosing what to work on, not for opening a change request, and not for deciding whether
the result is good enough — each of those is somebody else's job.

- agent-workflows:file-issue: Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the
words it was made in rather than paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone
else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to. - Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
"this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
"this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
"that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.

- agent-workflows:gen-readme: Writes a project's README from the code: researches current README convention on the
web, studies the repo from its ground truth rather than its existing docs, finds the key
points a newcomer needs first, draws every one of them as an SVG rendered to PNG, and
writes the file. Produces the README only — it does not open a PR, and review-readme
gates what it wrote. - Use whenever a README is about to be created or edited — before writing one from
scratch, and before changing an existing one. Covers "write the README", "generate a
README for this project", "our README is stale, redo it", "update the README", "document
this repo for newcomers", "write a README for ../other-repo" — and applies even when the
request is to touch one section rather than the whole file.

- agent-workflows:land-pr: Merges an approved change request and cleans up after it: the code lands in the default
branch, the branch is gone, the issue closes, the labels clear. Asks a person outright
whether the change was reviewed and tested at this exact head, records that answer, and
pins the merge to that SHA so a head that moved cannot slip through. Refuses to merge
without the answer. - Use when an open change request should land — "merge it", "merge PR 30", "land it",
"ship it", "close out #27", "the PR is approved", "merge and clean up". Being told to run
this is a request to reach the human gate, never the answer to it. Not for opening a
change request, and not for work that ends in evidence rather than a diff.

- agent-workflows:open-pr: Pushes a committed branch and opens the change request that carries it to a human, linked
to its issue so the issue closes on merge rather than by hand. Moves the commits onto a
branch first when they landed on the default one, gets the closure keyword right, and
stops for review. It does not merge, and it does not judge whether the work is good;
something before it did that. - Use when reviewed work is ready for a human to look at — "open a PR", "raise the merge
request", "push this up", "ship it", "put it up for review", "my commits are on main, get
them onto a branch". Reach for it after the work has been judged done, and when someone
says ship it meaning make it reviewable. Not for work that ends in evidence rather than a
diff, which closes on its issue and never reaches a change request. Not for merging.

- agent-workflows:plan-work: Splits work too large for one issue into issues that can each be delivered on their own,
and groups them with whatever the project already uses to group things — a milestone, a
project board, an epic. Decides first whether splitting is warranted at all, since most
work is not, and never invents a grouping the platform already provides. - Use when one issue is holding more than one deliverable — "break this down", "what are
the tasks", "this is too big", "split it", "that's really three things", "plan this
out", "make tickets for this". Also when take-issue reports that an issue is more than
one task, which is the case that arrives without anyone asking for a plan. Not for
ordinary work that happens to have several steps, and not for filing a single issue.

- agent-workflows:remove-stale-files: Finds and removes what this plugin's earlier versions wrote into a project: forked
commands and skills that shadow the placed units, rules and story files nothing reads
any more, and the sections this plugin wrote into `project-profile.md`. Shows every file
before touching one, and deletes only on a yes. It never adds: every edit it makes is a
removal. - Use whenever one of the files below is read, edited, or about to be created. Its
presence is the trigger; nobody has to ask for a cleanup. In `.claude/commands/`:
`dw-story`, `dw-plan`, `dw-tasks`, `dw-implement`, `dw-create-pr`, `dw-merge`,
`dw-review-story`, `dw-review-tasks`, `dw-review-implement`, `dw-review-pr`,
`dw-test-design`, `qw-plan`, `qw-cases`, `qw-review-plan`, `qw-review-cases`,
`qw-drift`. In `.claude/skills/`: `auditing-artifacts`, `auditing-readme`,
`ship-create-pr`, `ship-merge`, `reviewing-finish`, `doc-gen-readme`,
`doc-review-readme`, and a local copy of any name this plugin ships. In
`.claude/rules/`: `agent-report.md`, `anti-slop.md`, `dev-workflow.md`,
`doc-workflow.md`, `qa-workflow.md`, `ship-tail.md`, `profile-doctrine.md`, and the
sections this plugin wrote into `project-profile.md`. Elsewhere: `docs/stories/`,
`docs/agents/domain.md`, `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`,
`CONTEXT.md`, and a `## How to report` or `## Agent skills` section in `CLAUDE.md` or
`AGENTS.md`. Also on request: "clean up .claude", "why are there two ship-merge", "is
this rule still read", "we retired that workflow, what is left". …
- agent-workflows:reporting-outcomes: Reports work in two lines and a question — the verdict, the one next step, and whether
the reader wants it run or wants the detail. Findings, what was checked, risks and
decisions are prepared and held; the reader acts on the next step or asks. Only a
blocked or failed next step brings its blocker up with it. Replaces the reply that mixes
progress, findings, reasoning and status into a narrative the reader has to mine. - Use whenever writing back about work — what was done, what was found, whether it worked,
where things stand, what is left, what broke, what is blocked — and the answer runs
longer than a line. Covers the everyday reply, not only a formal gate: a status update,
a summary of a run, a review verdict, a handoff note, an answer to "how did it go" or
"where are we". Reach for it even when nobody said the word "report", even when the
reply feels short enough to wing, and even when the news is good. The buried verdict is
the failure this prevents, and it is invisible to the person writing it.

- agent-workflows:review-readme: Gates a README before a person reads it, on three counts: it delivers for a newcomer,
it is true to the code, and it reads and looks right. Derives the key points from the
code and checks the README leads with them and ships a diagram for each, verifies every
command, path, env var and link against the source, and re-renders each diagram to catch
one that has drifted from what it is drawn from. Gates what gen-readme wrote, and any
README edited by hand. - Use whenever a README has just been created or edited, by this toolkit or by hand —
including an edit made without gen-readme, and an edit to a single section rather than
the whole file. Also on request: "review the README", "check the README is accurate",
"does the README still match the code", "gate this README before I open a PR". A README
changed and not gated reaches its reader unverified, so treat any write to one as the
trigger rather than waiting to be asked.

- agent-workflows:review-work: Judges what state finished work is actually in, and routes it there. Checks the
acceptance line against the work rather than against the claim about it, sweeps what the
change left behind, and sends the result onward, back for more, back to the issue, or up
for splitting. Only one of its five outcomes reaches a change request, which is the point
of having it. - Use after work has been done and before anything ships it, every time, whatever kind it
is. Triggers: "review this", "check my work", "is this done", "did that work", "have a
look", "ready to ship?", and the end of any do-task run. Reach for it on evidence work
too, where there is no diff to read and the question is whether the act is proven. Not
for judging prose or a document's look, and not for opening a change request.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-artifacts: Gates the tooling an agent reads — skills, commands, rules, CLAUDE.md — asking whether
the file has one clear job, delivers it end to end, leaves the choices the project owns
to the project, matches the repo as it actually is, and can be followed without guessing.
Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT. CUT is the verdict nothing else makes: this artifact
duplicates another or does nothing, and should be removed. - Use whenever a file an agent reads is written or changed — a SKILL.md, a slash command, a
rules file, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md — and before adding a new one to a collection, since
the overlap question is easiest to answer while it is still cheap. Also on request:
"review this skill", "is this command any good", "does this rule earn its place", "why
isn't my skill triggering", "do we need both of these". Judges whether the artifact does
its job; the look and the words of a human-read document are a different review.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-phrasing: Reviews the words of a document a person will read, and returns PASS or REVISE. Starts
by establishing what the file actually is and who reads it, because a markdown file
carries no contract the way a source file does, and the same wording is correct in a
talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical
tells by grep rather than by impression, and judges what a pattern cannot reach. - Use whenever prose a person will read is written or edited: a README, a design doc or
RFC, a test plan, a QA report, a bug report, API or CLI reference, release notes, slide
content, a demo script. Also on request: "does this read okay", "make this clearer",
"tighten this up", "write this up", "too wordy". Reach for it on a document that is
factually correct and still hard to read, and on any document an agent generated, which
is the case that most needs it and least asks for it.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-typography: Reviews how a human-read document looks — a README, prose and tables in docs/, an HTML
page — and returns PASS or REVISE. Works the way a UI designer does: group the content,
space the groups so the inner gap is smaller than the outer one, emphasize by dimming
what is not the point rather than shouting what is, hold the level count low, and judge
the page whole rather than section by section. Judges the look; the words are a separate
review. - Use whenever a document a person will read is written or restructured — a README, a
guide, release notes, an HTML page — and before it reaches its reader. Also on request:
"does this read okay", "make this scannable", "why does this look like a wall", "clean
up the formatting", "too many headings". Reach for it on a doc that is factually right
and still hard to get through, which is the case nobody thinks to ask about.

- agent-workflows:take-issue: Picks up a tracked issue of any kind and claims it: resolves which one, reads it whole
along with the log it links, judges whether it can actually be started, and refuses it
back when it cannot. Assigns it, moves the state label, cuts a branch where a diff is
coming, and stops before any work begins — so a misreading is catchable while it is still
cheap. The read half of an issue; something else does the work. - Use whenever work is about to start on something already tracked, whatever kind it is —
"work on #42", "what's next", "pick something up", "grab the next one", "I'll take that",
"what should I do now". Code: "start on the parser bug". Docs: "fix that README issue".
Environment: "do the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate that cert", "run the
migration", "take the cert one". Reach for it before any work begins, not only before
code — an operation issue is claimed the same way and is the case most likely to be
started without ever being picked up. Reach for it even when the issue number is known
and the work looks obvious, because the point is to read the issue rather than to
remember it. Not for filing something new, and not for doing the work once claimed.

- mattpocock-skills:grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.

- agent-workflows-runner:review-ci-system: Judges what a project's tests actually prove, rather than how many there are. Classifies
every test by what it is allowed to touch, discards the levels that cannot answer
"is this covered", and lays the rest against what the system must do — so a suite that is
large, tidy and green is still reported as proving nothing when that is the truth. Writes
no test and deletes none; it names the one gap worth closing and stops. - Use whenever someone touches the machinery that tests or runs a project — creates a test
file, edits one, reads one, deletes one, adds or edits a CI workflow — and whenever the
question is what the tests are worth: "is this covered", "are these tests any good", "do
the tests actually test anything", "the suite is green but it broke in production", "why
did this ship broken", "review our test setup", "what's our coverage". Reach for it before
writing a new test, because what to write is decided by what is missing, and before
trusting a green suite, which is the case that never asks for review. Not for running the

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. - artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.

1	import { buildApp } from './app.js'
2	import { expectedTestLinkMcp, McpTestLinkClient } from './mcp-testlink-client.js'
3	import { connectToPostgres, PostgresStore } from './postgres-store.js'
4	import { required } from './setting.js'
5	import { connectToTestLinkMcp } from './stdio-tool-caller.js'
6	
7	/**
8	 * The database, which holds the Rules and the Reference Documents. Read only
9	 * from here: what is in it was written by an operator with SQL, and this project
10	 * ships nothing that writes to it (ADR-0006).
11	 */
12	const store = new PostgresStore(await connectToPostgres(required('DATABASE_URL')))
13	
14	/**
15	 * Read once, here, and never again — the property ADR-0004 keeps when it moves
16	 * Rules out of a file. A database with none enabled in it is missing in the same
17	 * way an invalid Rule is: there is no point starting a server that would accept
18	 * every write it is given.
19	 */
20	const rules = await store.rules()
21	
22	if (rules.length === 0) {
23	  throw new Error(
24	    'No enabled Rules are in the database, so the server will not start. Apply schema.sql and insert a Rule — the README has the statements.',
25	  )
26	}
27	
28	/**
29	 * How to launch testlink-mcp. It documents two ways of being run — the
30	 * published container and a checkout of its source — so both are reachable
31	 * here; the container is the default because it is the documented one. The
32	 * arguments are read as JSON so that a path with a space in it survives, which
33	 * is also the shape every MCP client configuration writes them in.
34	 *
35	 * The container is pinned to the version the client calls rather than tracking
36	 * `latest`. A tag is not a version: Docker will not re-pull one it already
37	 * holds, so `latest` is whatever it meant the first time a host pulled it, and
38	 * a host that pulled before a tool existed keeps a server without it.
39	 */
40	function testLinkMcp(): { command: string; args: string[] } {
41	  const command = process.env.TESTLINK_MCP_COMMAND
42	
43	  if (command === undefined) {
44	    return {
45	      command: 'docker',
46	      args: [
47	        'run',
48	        '--rm',
49	        '-i',
50	        '-e',
51	        'TESTLINK_URL',
52	        '-e',
53	        'TESTLINK_API_KEY',
54	        `dogkeeper886/testlink-mcp:${expectedTestLinkMcp}`,
55	      ],
56	    }
57	  }
58	
59	  try {
60	    return { command, args: JSON.parse(required('TESTLINK_MCP_ARGS')) }
61	  } catch (error) {
62	    throw new Error(
63	      `TESTLINK_MCP_ARGS must be a JSON list of arguments, so the server will not start: ${
64	        (error as Error).message
65	      }`,
66	    )
67	  }
68	}
69	
70	const tools = await connectToTestLinkMcp({
71	  ...testLinkMcp(),
72	  env: {
73	    ...process.env,
74	    TESTLINK_URL: required('TESTLINK_URL'),
75	    TESTLINK_API_KEY: required('TESTLINK_API_KEY'),
76	  } as Record<string, string>,
77	})
78	
79	const app = buildApp({
80	  testlink: new McpTestLinkClient(tools, { authorLogin: required('TESTLINK_AUTHOR_LOGIN') }),
81	  documents: store,
82	  rules,
83	  // Violations and outages, and not a line per request: what is logged is what
84	  // an operator is meant to read, and request logging was not asked for.
85	  logger: { level: 'warn' },
86	})
87	
88	await app.listen({ port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), host: '0.0.0.0' })

1	import Fastify, {
2	  type FastifyError,
3	  type FastifyInstance,
4	  type FastifyReply,
5	  type FastifyRequest,
6	  type FastifyServerOptions,
7	} from 'fastify'
8	
9	import type { DocumentStore } from './reference-document.js'
10	import { bindRules, ruleSetVersionOf, type StoredRule } from './rule-set.js'
11	import type {
12	  NewProject,
13	  NewTestSuite,
14	  ProjectChanges,
15	  TestCase,
16	  TestLinkClient,
17	  TestSuiteChanges,
18	} from './testlink-client.js'
19	import { findViolations, type Violation } from './violation.js'
20	
21	/**
22	 * The Field structure of a Test Case. A submission that does not match it is
23	 * refused before any Rule evaluation runs. `satisfies` keeps the schema and the
24	 * TestCase type from drifting apart: a Field added to one must appear in both.
25	 */
26	const testCaseSchema = {
27	  type: 'object',
28	  required: ['name', 'summary'],
29	  additionalProperties: false,
30	  properties: {
31	    name: { type: 'string' },
32	    summary: { type: 'string' },
33	    preconditions: { type: 'string' },
34	  },
35	} as const satisfies {
36	  type: 'object'
37	  required: readonly (keyof TestCase)[]
38	  additionalProperties: false
39	  properties: Record<keyof Required<TestCase>, { type: string }>
40	}
41	
42	/** The settings a Project carries, shared by the shapes that create and change one. */
43	const projectSettings = {
44	  notes: { type: 'string' },
45	  active: { type: 'boolean' },
46	  isPublic: { type: 'boolean' },
47	  requirementsEnabled: { type: 'boolean' },
48	  testPriorityEnabled: { type: 'boolean' },
49	  automationEnabled: { type: 'boolean' },
50	  inventoryEnabled: { type: 'boolean' },
51	} as const
52	
53	/** What a caller says about a Project it is creating. */
54	const newProjectSchema = {
55	  type: 'object',
56	  required: ['name', 'prefix'],
57	  additionalProperties: false,
58	  properties: { name: { type: 'string' }, prefix: { type: 'string' }, ...projectSettings },
59	} as const satisfies {
60	  type: 'object'
61	  required: readonly (keyof NewProject)[]
62	  additionalProperties: false
63	  properties: Record<keyof Required<NewProject>, { type: string }>
64	}
65	
66	/**
67	 * What a caller may change about a Project. At least one, because TestLink
68	 * refuses a change that names none and a caller reads that as its own mistake
69	 * sooner if it is refused here.
70	 */
71	const projectChangesSchema = {
72	  type: 'object',
73	  minProperties: 1,
74	  additionalProperties: false,
75	  properties: { name: { type: 'string' }, color: { type: 'string' }, ...projectSettings },
76	} as const satisfies {
77	  type: 'object'
78	  minProperties: number
79	  additionalProperties: false
80	  properties: Record<keyof Required<ProjectChanges>, { type: string }>
81	}
82	
83	/**
84	 * Deleting a Project takes everything under it, so the caller restates the
85	 * Project's own prefix and the delete is refused without it.
86	 */
87	const deleteProjectSchema = {
88	  type: 'object',
89	  required: ['confirmPrefix'],
90	  additionalProperties: false,
91	  properties: { confirmPrefix: { type: 'string' } },
92	} as const
93	
94	/**
95	 * What a caller says about a Test Suite it is creating, and where to put it.
96	 * Held to the same drift check as the Test Case schema above.
97	 */
98	const newTestSuiteSchema = {
99	  type: 'object',
100	  required: ['name'],
101	  additionalProperties: false,
102	  properties: {
103	    name: { type: 'string' },
104	    details: { type: 'string' },
105	    parentSuiteId: { type: 'string' },
106	  },
107	} as const satisfies {
108	  type: 'object'
109	  required: readonly (keyof NewTestSuite)[]
110	  additionalProperties: false
111	  properties: Record<keyof Required<NewTestSuite> | 'parentSuiteId', { type: string }>
112	}
113	
114	/** What a caller may change about a Test Suite. Its place in the Project is not one of them. */
115	const testSuiteChangesSchema = {
116	  type: 'object',
117	  additionalProperties: false,
118	  properties: {
119	    name: { type: 'string' },
120	    details: { type: 'string' },
121	  },
122	} as const satisfies {
123	  type: 'object'
124	  additionalProperties: false
125	  properties: Record<keyof Required<TestSuiteChanges>, { type: string }>
126	}
127	
128	export function buildApp({
129	  testlink,
130	  documents,
131	  rules,
132	  logger = false,
133	}: {
134	  testlink: TestLinkClient
135	  /** Where the Reference Documents are read from. Read only — nothing here writes one. */
136	  documents: DocumentStore
137	  /** The operator's enabled Rules, as the database holds them. Bound once here and never re-read. */
138	  rules: StoredRule[]
139	  /**
140	   * Where the server logs, off unless the entry point turns it on. Logs are
141	   * observability alone: nothing written here is read back, and no logged data
142	   * reaches a validation outcome.
143	   */
144	  logger?: FastifyServerOptions['logger']
145	}): FastifyInstance {
146	  // Binding happens before the server exists, so an invalid Rule leaves nothing
147	  // to call rather than a server running without its Rules.
148	  const bound = bindRules(rules)
149	
150	  // Fixed for the life of the process, because the Rules are read once and
151	  // never reloaded.
152	  const ruleSetVersion = ruleSetVersionOf(rules)
153	
154	  // Coercion off: a Field of the wrong type is refused, not quietly converted
155	  // into one that passes.
156	  const app = Fastify({ logger, ajv: { customOptions: { coerceTypes: false } } })
157	
158	  // The envelope names the Rules this server is running, on every answer without
159	  // exception — a delete, which has no body to carry them, included.
160	  app.addHook('onSend', async (_request, reply) => {
161	    reply.header('Rule-Set-Version', ruleSetVersion)
162	  })
163	
164	  /**
165	   * The version in the answer itself, where the Rules judged what was sent.
166	   * Callers are agents that read the body, so an answer the Rules took part in
167	   * names them in it rather than only on the envelope. An answer no Rule reached
168	   * — a schema refusal, or content TestLink did not hold — carries no version in
169	   * its body, because the Rules contributed nothing to it.
170	   */
171	  const versioned = <T extends object>(body: T) => ({ ...body, ruleSetVersion })
172	
173	  /**
174	   * A Rejection, and the log lines that make a Rule firing over and over
175	   * visible — the signal separating a Rule that cannot be satisfied from an
176	   * agent that writes badly once. Nothing is counted here and nothing is read
177	   * back, so the same Test Case submitted twice is answered identically.
178	   */
179	  const reject = (request: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply, violations: Violation[]) => {
180	    for (const { field, rule } of violations) {
181	      request.log.warn({ ruleSetVersion, field, rule }, 'Rule violated')
182	    }
183	
184	    return reply.code(422).send(versioned({ violations }))
185	  }
186	
187	  // A schema refusal carries no violations, so it cannot be read as a Rejection.
188	  app.setErrorHandler((error: FastifyError, _request, reply) => {
189	    if (error.validation) {
190	      return reply.code(400).send({ refusal: 'schema', message: error.message })
191	    }
192	    return reply.send(error)
193	  })
194	
195	  /**
196	   * What TestLink holds nothing under is the caller's to correct, so it answers
197	   * as a client error — where TestLink being unreachable, which is the server's

6	/** A Field of a Test Case. */

9	/** A Field of a Reference Document. */
10	export type ReferenceDocumentField = keyof Required<ReferenceDocument>

12	/** Any Field a Rule Set can be bound to, whichever content it is a part of. */

15	/**

17	 * makes drift a type error: a Field added to `TestCase` or to
18	 * `ReferenceDocument` must be added here too.
19	 */
20	const fieldNames = {
21	  testCase: Object.keys({
22	    name: null,
23	    summary: null,
24	    preconditions: null,
25	  } satisfies Record<TestCaseField, null>),
26	  referenceDocument: Object.keys({
27	    title: null,
28	    body: null,
29	  } satisfies Record<ReferenceDocumentField, null>),

32	/**
33	 * What the content is called where an operator reads it, so a report names the
34	 * thing the Rule Set failed to bind to rather than the key it was written under.
35	 */
36	const contentNames: Record<ContentKind, string> = {
37	  testCase: 'a Test Case',
38	  referenceDocument: 'a Reference Document',
39	}

41	/** The kinds of content Rule Sets bind to, which is what the source names first. */
42	export type ContentKind = keyof typeof fieldNames

44	function isContentKind(name: string): name is ContentKind {

48	/** The Rules bound to a single Field. */

51	/**

53	 * to. The two are kept apart rather than sharing one namespace: a Rule Set
54	 * written under the wrong content is then refused at startup instead of binding
55	 * to nothing and quietly never firing.

61	/** The Fields the named content has, as the type of its Rule Set keys. */
62	type FieldsOf<Kind extends ContentKind> = Kind extends 'testCase'

64	  : ReferenceDocumentField

66	/** One check applied to one Field. */

69	/** Matches a word or phrase, as written but in any casing. */
70	export interface TermRule extends RuleIdentity {
71	  type: 'term'
72	  term: string
73	}
74	
75	/** Matches a single character, optionally only where whitespace flanks it. */
76	export interface SymbolRule extends RuleIdentity {
77	  type: 'symbol'
78	  symbol: string
79	  flanked?: 'whitespace'

82	interface RuleIdentity {
83	  id: string
84	  reason: string

88	   * is no shared exception list, because a shared list drifts away from the

94	/**

96	 * enabled Exceptions. The reader above speaks in these rather than in rows, so
97	 * the SQL stays in the store and what is bound here is what was read.

101	 * type cannot be trusted about what a database answered with.

104	  ruleId: string
105	  contentKind: string
106	  field: string
107	  category: string
108	  looksFor: string
109	  flanked: string | null
110	  reason: string
111	  exceptions: string[]

114	/**
115	 * Checks one stored Rule, answering either the Rule or the problem to report.
116	 * The Rule is rebuilt from the values that were checked, so nothing unchecked is
117	 * bound.
118	 *
119	 * Every problem below is already a CHECK constraint in `schema.sql`, which
120	 * refuses the row at insert while the operator is present to fix it. This is
121	 * what stands between a database those constraints were never applied to and a
122	 * server that binds a Rule to a Field it was not written for: it reports, and
123	 * the server does not start.
124	 */
125	function checkStoredRule(stored: StoredRule): Rule | string {
126	  const { ruleId, contentKind, field, category, looksFor, flanked, reason, exceptions } = stored
127	  const at = `${contentKind} / ${field} / ${ruleId === '' ? 'a Rule with no id' : ruleId}`
128	
129	  if (ruleId === '') {
130	    return `${at}: id is missing`
131	  }
132	
133	  if (!isContentKind(contentKind)) {
134	    return `${at}: Rules bind to a Test Case or a Reference Document, and this is neither`
135	  }

137	  if (!fieldNames[contentKind].includes(field)) {
138	    return `${at}: ${contentNames[contentKind]} has no Field by that name`
139	  }

141	  if (reason === '') {

145	  const identity: RuleIdentity = { id: ruleId, reason, exceptions }

154	    // stored as another.

157	    }

165	    }

167	    if (flanked === null) {
168	      return { ...identity, type: 'symbol', symbol: looksFor }
169	    }

173	    }

181	/**

183	 * them. Every problem is collected before any is reported, so an operator fixes
184	 * them together rather than one restart at a time.
185	 *

187	 * against — the same thing an empty Rule Set was.
188	 */
189	export function checkRules(stored: StoredRule[]): { bound: RuleSets; problems: string[] } {
190	  const bound: RuleSets = { testCase: new Map(), referenceDocument: new Map() }
191	  const problems: string[] = []
192	
193	  for (const rule of stored) {
194	    const checked = checkStoredRule(rule)
195	
196	    if (typeof checked === 'string') {
197	      problems.push(checked)
198	      continue
199	    }
200	
201	    // `checkStoredRule` has just established that this row names one of the two
202	    // kinds and a Field that kind has.
203	    const ruleSets = bound[rule.contentKind as ContentKind] as Map<string, RuleSet>
204	    const ruleSet = ruleSets.get(rule.field)
205	
206	    if (ruleSet === undefined) {
207	      ruleSets.set(rule.field, [checked])
208	      continue

211	    ruleSet.push(checked)
212	  }

214	  return { bound, problems }

217	/**
218	 * Binds stored Rules, refusing to start where anything is wrong with them. This
219	 * is the startup path: there is no point starting a server that would refuse or
220	 * misplace every write it is given.

222	export function bindRules(stored: StoredRule[]): RuleSets {
223	  const { bound, problems } = checkRules(stored)

225	  if (problems.length > 0) {

232	/**

234	 * Field and the Rule at fault, so it is read without reading a stack trace.
235	 */
236	function refuse(problems: string[]): never {

242	/**
243	 * Names the Rules in force, so a Violation traces to the Rules that produced it

245	 * the Rules themselves rather than declared beside them: a version an operator
246	 * types goes on naming Rules that have since been changed, which is the
247	 * confusion a version is kept to prevent.
248	 *
249	 * It covers everything a caller was judged by and nothing else. Disabled Rules
250	 * never reach here — they judge nothing — so switching one off and later back on
251	 * returns the version to what it was rather than to a new one meaning the same
252	 * thing. Neither the row's id nor the order the database answered in is part of
253	 * it, for the same reason: neither is something a caller was judged by.
254	 *
255	 * The Rule's own id is, though it is not looked for in a Field: it is what a
256	 * Violation carries, so a version that ignored it would name two Rule Sets a
257	 * caller reads differently as one.

260	  const canonical = stored

263	        contentKind,
264	        field,
265	        ruleId,
266	        category,
267	        looksFor,
268	        flanked,
269	        reason,
270	        [...exceptions].sort(),
271	      ]),
272	    )
273	    .sort()
274	    .join('\n')
275	
276	  return createHash('sha256').update(canonical).digest('hex').slice(0, 12)
277	}

3	/**

10	  /** The id the operator gave the Rule, which tells two Rules on one Field apart. */
11	  rule: string
12	  reason: string
13	  /** The text that matched, and where it starts in the Field. */
14	  text: string

18	/**
19	 * Every Violation a piece of content produces. Fields are checked
20	 * independently, and each Field against every Rule bound to it, so the caller
21	 * corrects in one pass rather than resubmitting to discover the next problem.
22	 *
23	 * Written against Fields rather than against a Test Case, because a Reference
24	 * Document has Fields too and is checked the same way. The caller passes the
25	 * Rule Sets bound to that content, so a Rule can only ever reach a Field of the
26	 * content it was written for.
27	 */
28	export function findViolations<Field extends FieldName>(
29	  content: Partial<Record<Field, string>>,
30	  ruleSets: Map<Field, RuleSet>,
31	): Violation[] {
32	  const found: Violation[] = []
33	
34	  for (const [field, rules] of ruleSets) {
35	    const value = content[field]
36	
37	    if (value === undefined) {
38	      continue
39	    }
40	
41	    for (const rule of rules) {
42	      const fired =
43	        rule.type === 'term'
44	          ? termViolations(field, value, rule)
45	          : symbolViolations(field, value, rule)
46	
47	      // Suppression is applied per Rule, with only that Rule's own Exceptions,
48	      // so an Exception cannot reach a Rule it was not written for.
49	      const suppressed = suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)
50	
51	      found.push(...fired.filter((violation) => !isSuppressed(violation, suppressed)))
52	    }
53	  }
54	
55	  return found
56	}

58	/** Where a word or phrase was found in a Field. */

61	  end: number

64	/**
65	 * Where this Rule's Exceptions reach in the Field. An Exception is written the
66	 * way a Term is and found the same way — in any casing, however its words are
67	 * spaced — but it is found wherever it turns up, inside a longer word included:
68	 * an operator writing `guest-*` to permit a wildcard SSID means the characters
69	 * they wrote, and a Rule that fires on `guest-*1` has not been excepted.
70	 */

72	  return exceptions.flatMap((exception) => spansOf(value, exception))

75	/**
76	 * Whether an Exception covers the whole of what the Rule matched. Suppression
77	 * is by where the match falls, not by what the Field contains elsewhere: an
78	 * Exception permits the narrow case it names and leaves the rest of the Field
79	 * under the Rule.
80	 */
81	function isSuppressed(violation: Violation, spans: Span[]): boolean {
82	  const { offset, text } = violation
83	
84	  return spans.some((span) => offset >= span.start && offset + text.length <= span.end)

87	/** Every place a Term Rule fires in one Field. */

106	/** Every place a word or phrase turns up in a Field, as a Term is read. */

122	 */
123	function matcherFor(term: string): RegExp {
124	  const literal = term.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')
125	
126	  return new RegExp(literal.replace(/\s+/g, '\\s+'), 'giu')
127	}
128	
129	/**
130	 * Whether the match stands as a word rather than sitting inside a longer one.
131	 * This is what separates a Term from a Symbol: banning `utilise` leaves
132	 * `utilises` alone, where banning a character finds it anywhere.
133	 */
134	function standsAsWord(value: string, offset: number, text: string): boolean {
135	  return isOutsideAWord(value[offset - 1]) && isOutsideAWord(value[offset + text.length])
136	}
137	
138	/**
139	 * Anything a word does not run through, the edge of the Field included. A word
140	 * runs through a hyphen and an underscore, so banning `associates` leaves
141	 * `re-associates` alone — the same reading of a word the Symbol Rules take.
142	 */
143	function isOutsideAWord(character: string | undefined): boolean {
144	  return character === undefined || !/[\p{L}\p{N}_-]/u.test(character)
145	}
146	
147	/** Every place a Symbol Rule fires in one Field. */
148	function symbolViolations(field: FieldName, value: string, rule: SymbolRule): Violation[] {
149	  const found: Violation[] = []
150	  const { symbol } = rule
151	
152	  for (
153	    let offset = value.indexOf(symbol);
154	    offset !== -1;
155	    offset = value.indexOf(symbol, offset + symbol.length)
156	  ) {
157	    if (rule.flanked === 'whitespace' && !flankedByWhitespace(value, offset, symbol)) {
158	      continue
159	    }
160	
161	    found.push({ field, rule: rule.id, reason: rule.reason, text: symbol, offset })
162	  }
163	
164	  return found
165	}
166	
167	/**
168	 * Whether whitespace surrounds the Symbol. The edge of the Field counts as
169	 * whitespace: a Symbol opening or closing a Field is filler punctuation in the
170	 * same way one mid-sentence is, and it is still not inside a word.
171	 */
172	function flankedByWhitespace(value: string, offset: number, symbol: string): boolean {
173	  return isGap(value[offset - 1]) && isGap(value[offset + symbol.length])
174	}
175	
176	/** Whitespace, or the edge of the Field. */
177	function isGap(character: string | undefined): boolean {
178	  return character === undefined || /\s/.test(character)
179	}

1	import pg from 'pg'
2	
3	import type { Queries } from './queries.js'
4	import type {
5	  DocumentStore,
6	  ListedReferenceDocument,
7	  ReferenceDocument,
8	} from './reference-document.js'
9	import type { StoredRule } from './rule-set.js'
10	
11	/**
12	 * Whether an operator has applied `schema.sql` to this database. Asked outright
13	 * rather than read out of the error a missing table would raise: absence is told
14	 * from unreachability by what the database says about itself, never by matching
15	 * the text of a failure.
16	 */
17	async function hasSchema(queries: Queries): Promise<boolean> {
18	  const rows = await queries.run(
19	    "select 1 from information_schema.tables where table_name = 'rules'",
20	  )
21	
22	  return rows.length > 0
23	}
24	
25	/**
26	 * The enabled Exceptions, gathered under the Rule each belongs to. Read in a
27	 * statement of its own rather than joined: a Rule with no Exception is the
28	 * common one, and a join would answer for it with a row of nulls to tell apart
29	 * from a row carrying a phrase.
30	 */
31	async function exceptionsByRule(queries: Queries): Promise<Map<number, string[]>> {
32	  const rows = await queries.run(
33	    'select rule, phrase from rule_exceptions where enabled order by id',
34	  )
35	  const byRule = new Map<number, string[]>()
36	
37	  for (const row of rows) {
38	    const rule = Number(row.rule)
39	    const phrases = byRule.get(rule)
40	
41	    if (phrases === undefined) {
42	      byRule.set(rule, [String(row.phrase)])
43	      continue
44	    }
45	
46	    phrases.push(String(row.phrase))
47	  }
48	
49	  return byRule
50	}
51	
52	/**
53	 * The database, read only. This project makes no write to it at all (ADR-0006),
54	 * so there is no method here that could relax a Rule or author a Reference
55	 * Document — the server holds an object that cannot do either.
56	 *
57	 * Absence is an answer rather than a failure: a document the database holds
58	 * nothing under answers `undefined`, where the database being unreachable
59	 * throws out of `pg` and reaches the caller as a server error.
60	 */
61	export class PostgresStore implements DocumentStore {
62	  constructor(private readonly queries: Queries) {}
63	
64	  /**
65	   * The enabled Rules, each carrying its enabled Exceptions. Read once at
66	   * startup and never again, which is the property ADR-0004 keeps: a running
67	   * server judges every Test Case by the Rules it started with.
68	   *
69	   * A disabled Rule is not read at all. It stops firing exactly as completely as
70	   * a deleted one would, and its row stays so a Violation logged against it can
71	   * still be explained (ADR-0007).
72	   *
73	   * A database the schema has never been applied to has no tables at all, which
74	   * is still "no Rules" and not an outage — so it answers none here and the
75	   * server says what to do, rather than dying on a missing table.
76	   */
77	  async rules(): Promise<StoredRule[]> {
78	    if (!(await hasSchema(this.queries))) {
79	      return []
80	    }
81	
82	    const rows = await this.queries.run(
83	      'select id, rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, flanked, reason from rules where enabled order by id',
84	    )
85	    const exceptions = await exceptionsByRule(this.queries)
86	
87	    return rows.map((row) => ({
88	      ruleId: String(row.rule_id),
89	      contentKind: String(row.content_kind),
90	      field: String(row.field),
91	      category: String(row.category),
92	      looksFor: String(row.looks_for),
93	      // The column is nullable, and only a Symbol Rule ever carries it.
94	      flanked: row.flanked === null || row.flanked === undefined ? null : String(row.flanked),
95	      reason: String(row.reason),
96	      exceptions: exceptions.get(Number(row.id)) ?? [],
97	    }))
98	  }
99	
100	  async listDocuments(): Promise<ListedReferenceDocument[]> {
101	    const rows = await this.queries.run('select id, title from reference_documents order by id')
102	
103	    return rows.map((row) => ({ id: String(row.id), title: String(row.title) }))
104	  }
105	
106	  async getDocument(id: string): Promise<ReferenceDocument | undefined> {
107	    const [row] = await this.queries.run(
108	      'select title, body from reference_documents where id = $1',
109	      [id],
110	    )
111	
112	    return row === undefined ? undefined : { title: String(row.title), body: String(row.body) }
113	  }
114	}
115	
116	/** What this project needs of a connected client, which is one method of it. */
117	interface Connected {
118	  query(sql: string, parameters?: unknown[]): Promise<{ rows: unknown[] }>
119	}
120	
121	/**
122	 * Puts a connected client behind the statements-and-rows seam everything above
123	 * speaks in. Exported so that a test running an in-process Postgres reaches it
124	 * through this same adapter rather than through a copy of it.
125	 */
126	export function queriesFrom(client: Connected): Queries {
127	  return {
128	    async run(sql: string, parameters?: unknown[]) {
129	      const { rows } = await client.query(sql, parameters)
130	      return rows as Record<string, unknown>[]
131	    },
132	  }
133	}
134	
135	/**
136	 * Opens the one connection this process needs. Narrow by design: everything
137	 * above it speaks in statements and rows, so the store is exercised without a
138	 * database and this is the only part that needs one.
139	 */
140	export async function connectToPostgres(url: string): Promise<Queries & { close(): Promise<void> }> {
141	  const client = new pg.Client({ connectionString: url })
142	
143	  await client.connect()
144	
145	  return { ...queriesFrom(client), close: () => client.end() }
146	}
147

-- The tables this project owns, applied by an operator rather than by anything
-- the project ships (ADR-0006). The server only reads what is in them, so it is
-- never the thing that creates what it reads from.
--
--   psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f schema.sql
--
-- Safe to apply again: every statement asks for what it wants only if it is not
-- already there, so an operator unsure whether it has been applied can simply
-- apply it.

-- A Rule is a row (ADR-0007). It names the Field it binds to, the kind of check
-- it is, what it looks for, the reason it gives, and whether it is on. An
-- operator adds one Rule, or turns one off, with a statement naming that Rule
-- alone.
--
-- Nothing here is deleted. A Rule that should stop firing is disabled: it stops
-- firing just as completely, and the row stays so a Violation logged against it
-- can still be explained. The other half of the same discipline is that what a
-- Rule looks for is not edited either, because a changed check under an
-- unchanged name makes every Violation already logged describe something that
-- never happened. The reason is editable; it is what the caller is told, not
-- what is looked for.
--
-- Neither is enforced here, by decision rather than by oversight. The
-- constraints below refuse a Rule that is malformed, but a `delete` and a
-- rewritten `looks_for` are both ordinary SQL that this schema accepts.
-- Enforcing them takes a trigger, and a trigger stops the operator who does not
-- know the rule — of whom there are none, while there is one operator and it is
-- the maintainer. ADR-0007 records this, and records what to add on the day that
-- stops being true.
create table if not exists rules (
  id serial primary key,

  -- What a report calls this Rule. Unique per Field rather than overall: the
  -- same name on two Fields is two Rules, and both are worth having.
  rule_id text not null check (rule_id <> ''),
  content_kind text not null check (content_kind in ('testCase', 'referenceDocument')),
  field text not null,

  -- Which kind of check. A Term is a word or phrase matched in any casing; a
  -- Symbol is one character. `looks_for` holds whichever this Rule is.
  category text not null check (category in ('term', 'symbol')),
  looks_for text not null check (looks_for <> ''),

  -- Flanking narrows a Symbol Rule to where whitespace sits on both sides. Only
  -- a Symbol carries it.
  flanked text check (flanked = 'whitespace'),

  reason text not null check (reason <> ''),
  enabled boolean not null default true,
  added_at timestamptz not null default now(),

  unique (content_kind, field, rule_id),

  -- The Field has to belong to the content. Writing a Rule under the wrong one
  -- is refused here, while the operator is present, rather than at the next
  -- startup.
  constraint field_belongs_to_the_content check (
    (content_kind = 'testCase' and field in ('name', 'summary', 'preconditions'))
    or (content_kind = 'referenceDocument' and field in ('title', 'body'))
  ),

  -- `like '_'` is one character rather than one byte, which is the same reading
  -- the server makes: an em dash passes, and a mark carrying a variation
  -- selector — two code points, one glyph — does not.
  constraint a_symbol_is_one_character check (
    category <> 'symbol' or looks_for like '_'
  ),

  constraint only_a_symbol_is_flanked check (
    category <> 'term' or flanked is null
  )
);

-- The words and phrases that suppress one Rule where it would otherwise fire.
-- An Exception belongs to exactly one Rule; there is no shared list. Disabled
-- rather than deleted for the same reason a Rule is — removing one makes its
-- Rule fire where it previously did not, which is a change to what the Rules do.
create table if not exists rule_exceptions (
  id serial primary key,
  rule integer not null references rules (id),
  phrase text not null check (phrase <> ''),
  enabled boolean not null default true,
  added_at timestamptz not null default now(),

  unique (rule, phrase)
);

-- A Reference Document is its id, its title and its body — the id is what a
-- caller retrieves it by, and the title and the body are the two Fields the
-- Rules reach. The title is kept out of the body so a Rule firing in it is
-- reported once rather than under both Fields.
create table if not exists reference_documents (
  id text primary key,
  title text not null,
  body text not null,
  loaded_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

1	import type {
2	  NewProject,
3	  NewTestSuite,
4	  Placement,
5	  ProjectChanges,
6	  ProjectDeletion,
7	  TestCase,
8	  TestLinkClient,
9	  TestLinkContent,
10	  TestSuiteChanges,
11	} from './testlink-client.js'
12	import type { ToolCaller } from './tool-caller.js'
13	
14	/**
15	 * The real path to TestLink, through the testlink-mcp tools. Everything this
16	 * client does is one tool call and one reading of what came back, so the whole
17	 * of its judgement is in `answer` below: which failures are something that is
18	 * not there, and which are TestLink not answering at all.
19	 */
20	export class McpTestLinkClient implements TestLinkClient {
21	  constructor(
22	    private readonly tools: ToolCaller,
23	    /** Who the validator writes as. The one piece of TestLink identity a caller does not supply. */
24	    private readonly config: { authorLogin: string },
25	  ) {}
26	
27	  async createTestCase(
28	    { projectId, suiteId }: Placement,
29	    testCase: TestCase,
30	  ): Promise<{ id: string } | undefined> {
31	    const written = await this.answer('create_test_case', {
32	      data: {
33	        testprojectid: projectId,
34	        testsuiteid: suiteId,
35	        name: testCase.name,
36	        authorlogin: this.config.authorLogin,
37	        ...fieldsOf(testCase),
38	      },
39	    })
40	
41	    if (written === absent) {
42	      return undefined
43	    }
44	
45	    return { id: idOf(written, 'the Test Case it created') }
46	  }
47	
48	  async getTestCase(id: string): Promise<TestCase | undefined> {
49	    const held = await this.answer('read_test_case', { test_case_id: id })
50	
51	    if (held === absent) {
52	      return undefined
53	    }
54	
55	    // TestLink answers a read with the versions of a Test Case, and holds far
56	    // more about one than this project has Rules for. What is served is the
57	    // Fields, so a read answers a Test Case rather than a TestLink record.
58	    const version = first(held)
59	
60	    if (version === undefined) {
61	      return undefined
62	    }
63	
64	    return {
65	      name: text(version.name),
66	      summary: text(version.summary),
67	      preconditions: text(version.preconditions),
68	    }
69	  }
70	
71	  async updateTestCase(id: string, testCase: TestCase): Promise<boolean> {
72	    // A Field the caller left out is left out of the update: testlink-mcp
73	    // ignores an empty one, so an omission cannot clear what TestLink holds.
74	    const applied = await this.answer('update_test_case', {
75	      test_case_id: id,
76	      data: { name: testCase.name, ...fieldsOf(testCase) },
77	    })
78	
79	    return applied !== absent
80	  }
81	
82	  async deleteTestCase(id: string): Promise<boolean> {
83	    return (await this.answer('delete_test_case', { test_case_id: id })) !== absent
84	  }
85	
86	  async listProjects(): Promise<TestLinkContent> {
87	    const listed = await this.answer('list_projects', {})
88	
89	    if (listed === absent) {
90	      // Nothing was named to be missing, so TestLink reporting absence here is
91	      // TestLink not making sense rather than an answer a caller can act on.
92	      throw new Error('TestLink reported no Projects to list.')
93	    }
94	
95	    return listed
96	  }
97	
98	  async createProject(project: NewProject): Promise<{ id: string }> {
99	    const created = await this.answer('create_project', {
100	      name: project.name,
101	      prefix: project.prefix,
102	      ...settingsOf(project),
103	    })
104	
105	    if (created === absent) {
106	      // Nothing was named to be missing, so this is TestLink not making sense
107	      // rather than an answer a caller could act on.
108	      throw new Error('TestLink reported the Project it was asked to create as missing.')
109	    }
110	
111	    return { id: idOf(created, 'the Project it created') }
112	  }
113	
114	  async updateProject(projectId: string, changes: ProjectChanges): Promise<boolean> {
115	    const applied = await this.answer('update_project', {
116	      project_id: projectId,
117	      ...given({ name: changes.name }),
118	      ...settingsOf(changes),
119	    })
120	
121	    return applied !== absent
122	  }
123	
124	  async deleteProject(projectId: string, confirmPrefix: string): Promise<ProjectDeletion> {
125	    const deleted = await this.answer(
126	      'delete_project',
127	      { project_id: projectId, confirm_prefix: confirmPrefix },
128	      // The interlock refusing is the caller's to correct, so it is read here
129	      // rather than escalated: a caller told TestLink is down restates nothing.
130	      reportsUnconfirmed,
131	    )
132	
133	    if (deleted === unconfirmed) {
134	      return 'unconfirmed'
135	    }
136	
137	    return deleted === absent ? 'absent' : 'deleted'
138	  }
139	
140	  async listTestSuites(
141	    projectId: string,
142	    parentSuiteId?: string,
143	  ): Promise<TestLinkContent | undefined> {
144	    return this.listed('list_test_suites', {
145	      project_id: projectId,
146	      ...given({ parent_suite_id: parentSuiteId }),
147	    })
148	  }
149	
150	  async listTestCasesInSuite(suiteId: string): Promise<TestLinkContent | undefined> {
151	    return this.listed('list_test_cases_in_suite', { suite_id: suiteId })
152	  }
153	
154	  async createTestSuite(
155	    projectId: string,
156	    suite: NewTestSuite,
157	    parentSuiteId?: string,
158	  ): Promise<{ id: string } | undefined> {
159	    const created = await this.answer('create_test_suite', {
160	      project_id: projectId,
161	      suite_name: suite.name,
162	      ...given({ details: suite.details, parent_id: parentSuiteId }),
163	    })
164	
165	    if (created === absent) {
166	      return undefined
167	    }
168	
169	    return { id: idOf(created, 'the Test Suite it created') }
170	  }
171	
172	  async updateTestSuite(
173	    projectId: string,
174	    suiteId: string,
175	    changes: TestSuiteChanges,
176	  ): Promise<boolean> {
177	    const applied = await this.answer('update_test_suite', {
178	      suite_id: suiteId,
179	      project_id: projectId,
180	      data: changes,
181	    })
182	
183	    return applied !== absent
184	  }
185	
186	  async deleteTestSuite(suiteId: string): Promise<boolean> {
187	    return (await this.answer('delete_test_suite', { suite_id: suiteId })) !== absent
188	  }
189	
190	  /**
191	   * A listing of what TestLink holds under something the caller named. The
192	   * thing named not being there is an answer, the same as it is for a read:
193	   * a caller listing the Suites of a Project that is not there has an id to
194	   * correct, not an outage to escalate.
195	   */
196	  private async listed(
197	    tool: string,
198	    args: Record<string, unknown>,
199	  ): Promise<TestLinkContent | undefined> {
200	    const listed = await this.answer(tool, args)
201	
202	    return listed === absent ? undefined : listed
203	  }
204	
205	  /**
206	   * One tool call, read as one of three outcomes: what TestLink answered, the
207	   * thing named not being there, or a throw for everything else.
208	   *
209	   * Absence is read only out of what TestLink reported about the call — the
210	   * error it replied with, or the code-and-message it sometimes puts where a
211	   * result should go. It is never read out of served content, because a Test
212	   * Case is entitled to be about a file that does not exist and reading its own
213	   * words back as absence would make it disappear.
214	   *
215	   * Anything unreadable throws, so an unrecognised failure escalates as an
216	   * outage rather than being answered as absence: a caller told a Test Case is
217	   * not there stops looking for it.
218	   *
219	   * `alsoTheCallers` names one further failure this particular call's caller can
220	   * correct, for the calls that have one. It is read before absence, so a call
221	   * that fails for its own reason is not first mistaken for something missing.
222	   */
223	  private async answer(
224	    tool: string,
225	    args: Record<string, unknown>,
226	    alsoTheCallers?: (message: string) => boolean,
227	  ): Promise<TestLinkContent | typeof absent | typeof unconfirmed> {
228	    const result = await this.tools.call(tool, args)
229	
230	    if (result.isError) {
231	      return this.place(tool, result.text, alsoTheCallers)
232	    }
233	
234	    const content: unknown = JSON.parse(result.text)
235	    const reported = reportedProblem(content)
236	
237	    if (reported !== undefined) {
238	      return this.place(tool, reported, alsoTheCallers)
239	    }
240	
241	    const denied = deniedIn(content)
242	
243	    if (denied !== undefined) {
244	      throw new Error(`TestLink did not complete ${tool}: ${denied}`)
245	    }
246	
247	    return content
248	  }
249	
250	  /**
251	   * Which of the outcomes a caller can act on this failure is, or none of them,
252	   * in which case it escalates. Escalating is the default deliberately: a
253	   * failure nobody has taught this client to read is an outage until someone
254	   * has, because answering it as absence would send a caller away.
255	   */
256	  private place(
257	    tool: string,
258	    message: string,
259	    alsoTheCallers?: (message: string) => boolean,
260	  ): typeof absent | typeof unconfirmed {
261	    if (alsoTheCallers?.(message) === true) {
262	      return unconfirmed
263	    }
264	
265	    if (reportsMissingTool(message)) {
266	      throw new Error(
267	        `testlink-mcp does not provide ${tool}, so it is older than the ${expectedTestLinkMcp} this client calls: ${message}`,
268	      )
269	    }
270	
271	    if (reportsAbsence(message)) {
272	      return absent
273	    }
274	
275	    throw new Error(`TestLink could not be reached through ${tool}: ${message}`)
276	  }
277	}
278	
279	/** TestLink holds nothing under what the call named. */
280	const absent = Symbol('absent')
281	
282	/** The caller did not restate the Project's prefix, so TestLink deleted nothing. */
283	const unconfirmed = Symbol('unconfirmed')
284	
285	/**
286	 * The interlock refusing. TestLink asks a caller deleting a Project to restate
287	 * its prefix, and says so in its own words when the restatement does not match.
288	 */
289	function reportsUnconfirmed(message: string): boolean {
290	  return /Confirmation failed/i.test(message)
291	}
292	
293	/**
294	 * The arguments the caller actually gave, so an omission is left unsent rather
295	 * than sent empty. Only an omission is dropped: `false` and an empty string are
296	 * things a caller said, and a setting turned off has to reach TestLink as one.
297	 */
298	function given(args: Record<string, unknown>): Record<string, unknown> {
299	  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(args).filter(([, value]) => value !== undefined))
300	}
301	
302	/** The settings of a Project, as testlink-mcp names them. */
303	function settingsOf(project: NewProject | ProjectChanges): Record<string, unknown> {
304	  return given({
305	    notes: project.notes,
306	    active: project.active,
307	    is_public: project.isPublic,
308	    color: 'color' in project ? project.color : undefined,
309	    requirements_enabled: project.requirementsEnabled,
310	    test_priority_enabled: project.testPriorityEnabled,
311	    automation_enabled: project.automationEnabled,
312	    inventory_enabled: project.inventoryEnabled,
313	  })
314	}
315	
316	/** The Fields carrying content, as testlink-mcp takes them. */
317	function fieldsOf(testCase: TestCase): Record<string, string> {
318	  return { summary: testCase.summary, ...given({ preconditions: testCase.preconditions }) }
319	}
320	
321	/**
322	 * The id TestLink gave what it just created. TestLink reports it either at the
323	 * top of the result or in what it says about the operation, so both are read —
324	 * and a result carrying neither is a write that did not land, however
325	 * successfully it was phrased. Answering an id here is what makes the write
326	 * complete, so there is nothing to answer when TestLink named none.
327	 */
328	function idOf(content: TestLinkContent, subject: string): string {
329	  const created = first(content)
330	  const reported = record(created?.additionalInfo)
331	  const id = created?.id ?? reported?.id
332	
333	  // `0` and the empty string are ids nothing is held under, so they are read as
334	  // the absence of one rather than passed back for a caller to read with.
335	  if ((typeof id !== 'string' && typeof id !== 'number') || String(id) === '' || Number(id) === 0) {
336	    throw new Error(`TestLink reported no id for ${subject}: ${JSON.stringify(content)}`)
337	  }
338	
339	  return String(id)
340	}
341	
342	/**
343	 * The problem TestLink reported about a call it did not refuse outright.
344	 * TestLink answers some failures as a code and a message where the result
345	 * should be, rather than as an error, so both readings meet here. A reply
346	 * carrying no code is content, and is never read for a problem.
347	 */
348	function reportedProblem(content: unknown): string | undefined {
349	  const reported = first(content)
350	
351	  if (reported?.code === undefined || typeof reported.message !== 'string') {
352	    return undefined
353	  }
354	
355	  return reported.message
356	}
357	
358	/**
359	 * TestLink saying the operation did not happen. A write answers a caller only
360	 * once TestLink has confirmed it, and a reply that denies the write is not a
361	 * confirmation however cleanly it arrived. Only an explicit denial counts: a
362	 * reply that says nothing about status — every listing, and a read — is not
363	 * read as one.
364	 */
365	function deniedIn(content: unknown): string | undefined {
366	  const reported = first(content)
367	
368	  if (reported?.status !== false) {
369	    return undefined
370	  }
371	
372	  return typeof reported.message === 'string'
373	    ? reported.message
374	    : 'TestLink gave no reason for it.'
375	}
376	
377	/**
378	 * Whether TestLink is reporting that what the call named is not there. Two
379	 * wordings, because two things do the reporting: TestLink says a thing "does
380	 * not exist", and testlink-mcp says "not found" for the Projects it resolves
381	 * itself before calling TestLink at all. Both are matched narrowly, because
382	 * everything this does not match is escalated as an outage instead.
383	 */
384	function reportsAbsence(message: string): boolean {
385	  return /does not exist|not found/i.test(message)
386	}
387	
388	/**
389	 * The testlink-mcp this client is written against. It lives here because it is
390	 * the client that knows which tools it calls, and it is what launching the
391	 * server pins to, so the two cannot drift apart.
392	 */
393	export const expectedTestLinkMcp = '1.6.0'
394	
395	/**
396	 * Whether testlink-mcp is reporting a tool it does not have. A server older
397	 * than the version above answers this rather than failing anything in TestLink,
398	 * so it is the version showing through and not a word about TestLink, which is
399	 * reachable and healthy in every case that reaches here.
400	 */
401	function reportsMissingTool(message: string): boolean {
402	  return /Unknown tool/i.test(message)
403	}
404	
405	/** What TestLink sent, whether it sent one or a list of them. */
406	function first(content: unknown): Record<string, unknown> | undefined {
407	  return record(Array.isArray(content) ? content[0] : content)
408	}
409	
410	function record(value: unknown): Record<string, unknown> | undefined {
411	  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null ? (value as Record<string, unknown>) : undefined
412	}
413	
414	/** A Field as it is served: what TestLink holds, and empty where it holds nothing. */
415	function text(value: unknown): string {
416	  return typeof value === 'string' ? value : ''
417	}
418

1	/** A Test Case as submitted for validation and written through to TestLink. */
2	export interface TestCase {
3	  name: string
4	  summary: string
5	  preconditions?: string
6	}
7	
8	/**
9	 * Where in TestLink a Test Case is created. Supplied per submission rather than
10	 * fixed at deployment: TestLink is the store the caller works in, so which
11	 * Project and which Test Suite a case belongs to is the caller's to say.
12	 */
13	export interface Placement {
14	  projectId: string
15	  suiteId: string
16	}
17	
18	/**
19	 * What a caller says about a Project it is creating. The prefix is stamped into
20	 * every Test Case external id the Project ever holds, and TestLink will not
21	 * change it afterwards, so it is set here and appears in no change.
22	 */
23	export interface NewProject {
24	  name: string
25	  prefix: string
26	  notes?: string
27	  active?: boolean
28	  isPublic?: boolean
29	  requirementsEnabled?: boolean
30	  testPriorityEnabled?: boolean
31	  automationEnabled?: boolean
32	  inventoryEnabled?: boolean
33	}
34	
35	/** What a caller may change about a Project. Its prefix is not among them. */
36	export interface ProjectChanges {
37	  name?: string
38	  notes?: string
39	  active?: boolean
40	  isPublic?: boolean
41	  color?: string
42	  requirementsEnabled?: boolean
43	  testPriorityEnabled?: boolean
44	  automationEnabled?: boolean
45	  inventoryEnabled?: boolean
46	}
47	
48	/**
49	 * What became of a Project delete. Deleting a Project takes every Suite, Test
50	 * Case, Plan, Build, Execution and Requirement under it with it, so TestLink
51	 * asks the caller to restate the Project's own prefix before it does. Getting
52	 * that restatement wrong is the caller's to correct — it is told apart from the
53	 * Project not being there, and from TestLink not answering, because all three
54	 * would otherwise arrive as the same failure.
55	 */
56	export type ProjectDeletion = 'deleted' | 'absent' | 'unconfirmed'
57	
58	/** What a caller says about a Test Suite it is creating. */
59	export interface NewTestSuite {
60	  name: string
61	  details?: string
62	}
63	
64	/** What a caller may change about a Test Suite. Where it sits is not one of them. */
65	export interface TestSuiteChanges {
66	  name?: string
67	  details?: string
68	}
69	
70	/**
71	 * What TestLink reports about its own structure — Projects, Test Suites, and
72	 * the Test Cases a Suite holds. Left unmodelled because no Rule binds to it: it
73	 * is served on through, not checked, so giving it a shape here would invent
74	 * vocabulary the project does not have.
75	 */
76	export type TestLinkContent = unknown
77	
78	/**
79	 * The path to TestLink, read and write. Substituted in tests so the HTTP
80	 * surface can be exercised without a TestLink instance.
81	 *
82	 * Absence is an answer everywhere it can happen: an operation naming something
83	 * TestLink holds nothing under answers `undefined`, or `false` where it has no
84	 * content to answer with. Only TestLink being unreachable throws. Reporting the
85	 * two apart here is what lets every route answer them apart, rather than
86	 * reading an error message to guess which happened.
87	 *
88	 * The client reports content and never a judgement about it: what fired on that
89	 * content is decided by the Rules, above this interface.
90	 */
91	export interface TestLinkClient {
92	  /** Answers the id TestLink gave the Test Case, or nothing where it holds no such Test Suite. */
93	  createTestCase(placement: Placement, testCase: TestCase): Promise<{ id: string } | undefined>
94	  getTestCase(id: string): Promise<TestCase | undefined>
95	  /** Answers whether the Test Case was there to update. */
96	  updateTestCase(id: string, testCase: TestCase): Promise<boolean>
97	  /** Answers whether the Test Case was there to delete. */
98	  deleteTestCase(id: string): Promise<boolean>
99	
100	  listProjects(): Promise<TestLinkContent>
101	  /** Answers the id TestLink gave the Project. */
102	  createProject(project: NewProject): Promise<{ id: string }>
103	  /** Answers whether the Project was there to update. */
104	  updateProject(projectId: string, changes: ProjectChanges): Promise<boolean>
105	  /** Deletes a Project and everything under it, once the caller has restated its prefix. */
106	  deleteProject(projectId: string, confirmPrefix: string): Promise<ProjectDeletion>
107	  /** The Test Suites directly under a Project, or under `parentSuiteId` where one is named. */
108	  listTestSuites(projectId: string, parentSuiteId?: string): Promise<TestLinkContent | undefined>
109	  listTestCasesInSuite(suiteId: string): Promise<TestLinkContent | undefined>
110	
111	  /** Answers the id TestLink gave the Test Suite, or nothing where it holds no such Project. */
112	  createTestSuite(
113	    projectId: string,
114	    suite: NewTestSuite,
115	    parentSuiteId?: string,
116	  ): Promise<{ id: string } | undefined>
117	  /** Answers whether the Test Suite was there to update. */
118	  updateTestSuite(
119	    projectId: string,
120	    suiteId: string,
121	    changes: TestSuiteChanges,
122	  ): Promise<boolean>
123	  /** Answers whether the Test Suite was there to delete. */
124	  deleteTestSuite(suiteId: string): Promise<boolean>
125	}
