=== 0001-validation-is-outside-the-agent-trust-boundary.md ===
# Validation is outside the agent's trust boundary

The agent that generates test cases cannot reliably validate them at scenario
level, so validation is split into a separate service the generating agent
reaches only over HTTP. Rules are baked into the deployed image rather than read
from a mounted path, and there is no rule-reload endpoint — the agent has no
mechanism by which it could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it.

## Consequences

Rule changes require a rebuild and redeploy performed outside the generation
workflow. This is deliberate friction: a rule set the generating side can edit
is not a boundary.
=== 0002-detection-is-deterministic.md ===
# Detection is deterministic; the model never decides a violation

Every violation is produced by literal term or symbol matching, not by a language
model. A local model is used offline to survey the corpus and surface candidate
rules a human then writes; once written, that rule is deterministic forever and
the model has no further part in it.

## Considered Options

Running fields through a local model in the request path was the obvious reading
of "validation with Ollama" and was rejected. The API sits in a write path and
returns rejections an agent must act on, which requires verdicts that are
identical across runs and explainable to the person whose test case was refused.
A 9B model gives neither.

## Consequences

The model's role shrinks over time rather than growing — each rule promoted from
survey to rule set is one less thing needing inference. Detection classes that
cannot be expressed as literal matching (duplication, ambiguity, unstated
preconditions) are out of scope until a deterministic expression is found.
=== 0003-agent-works-only-over-the-api.md ===
# The generating agent works only over the API, never local files

The agent that creates test cases reads existing cases and reference documents
through this API, not from markdown or any other file on disk. It has no local
working copy of the corpus.

## Considered Options

Letting the agent keep local markdown was the obvious approach and was rejected.
Agents corrupt structured markdown reliably enough that skills and rules do not
prevent it, and a local copy is also a second source of truth that drifts from
TestLink. Serving everything over the API keeps one source of truth and leaves
the agent with no file it can quietly rewrite.

## Consequences

Reference documents must be reachable through the API, so document serving is in
scope for this project even though it is not validation. The read path becomes
the only channel by which the agent sees existing content, which makes it the
place where legacy fingerprints would otherwise propagate into new cases.
=== 0004-rule-sets-live-in-a-database.md ===
# Rule sets live in a database, read once at startup

Rule sets move out of YAML files and into a database. Only the store changes:
they are still read once when the server starts and never reloaded, so a running
server judges every test case by the rule sets it started with.

The database is not scoped to rule sets, and this ADR does not fix its scope.
The maintainer's framing is that it is where strictly validated content lands,
and that it may later become the source of truth imported into production
TestLink, or a cache in front of it. Those are open. What is settled here is that
rule sets are among the things it holds.

## Considered Options

**Files, kept in version control.** Argued for on the grounds that version
control already gives history, review before a rule can reject anything,
one-command rollback, and a rule set version derived from the text as supplied.
Rejected by the maintainer. The store this project already reaches for is a
server rather than a working copy — TestLink replaced the local test case
markdown files for the same reason — and the file argument answers for one rule
set at a time, where the pressure comes from many of them copied and tweaked from
each other.

## Consequences

**ADR-0001 no longer describes the store accurately.** It says rules are "baked
into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted path". Neither half will
be true. The property that ADR-0001 exists to protect survives unchanged: rule
sets are read once at startup, there is no reload endpoint, and the generating
agent reaches the server only over HTTP, so it still has no mechanism by which it
could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it. The README already flags this tension
as open pending deployment shape; that flag now resolves to a database.

**Rule Set Version is unaffected.** It stays derived from the rule sets as
supplied and fixed for the life of a running server, because reading once at
startup is exactly what is being kept.

**The server stops being stateless.** The README records "no storage layer... a
database waits until a real requirement for one appears". That wait is over, and
a component the project has so far done without now has to be run, backed up, and
reachable from the server at startup.
=== 0005-reference-documents-are-checked-content-in-the-database.md ===
# Reference documents are checked content, held in the database

> Partly superseded by ADR-0006. The "How content reaches the database" section
> below, and the consequence "There is one write path, and the server is not on
> it", are no longer how this works: there is no load command, and an operator
> writes with SQL. Everything else here still holds. The text is left as it was
> written, because what it records is the decision as it was taken.

Reference documents live in the database ADR-0004 introduced, and they are the
first thing to make that database real. They are composed of named fields the
way a test case is — a title and a body — each with its own rule set, so a read
carries the violations found in what it serves. They are read only: the API
lists them and retrieves one, and there is no endpoint that writes one.

This settles the question the README carried as open, "what the reference-document
endpoints look like", and it fixes one part of the scope ADR-0004 deliberately
left open.

## Considered Options

**Where the documents live.** A directory on the server, pointed at by an
environment variable the way rule sets were, was argued for on the grounds that
it ships immediately, needs no new infrastructure, and keeps the boundary that
matters — the agent has no local files, and the server having them is exactly
the trust boundary. Storing them in TestLink as requirement specifications was
argued for as keeping one source of truth. Both were rejected by the maintainer
in favour of building the ADR-0004 database now and making documents its first
tenant: the store was already decided, and a second temporary store would have
been a third place content lives.

**Whether a read reports violations.** Serving documents straight through,
unchecked, was argued for as the smaller change and the one that invents no
vocabulary: a rule set was defined as the rules bound to one field of a test
case, and a document had no fields. Rejected by the maintainer. ADR-0003's own
reasoning applies to documents at least as strongly as to test cases — the read
path is where legacy fingerprints propagate into new cases, and a reference
document written in the wording the rules exist to catch is the most direct way
for that to happen. Documents therefore gained fields so the rules could reach
them.

**Whether the agent can write a document.** Full CRUD, matching the test case
surface, was considered and rejected. A document the agent could write is a
document it could author in the style the rules catch and then read back as
authority, which is the same reason ADR-0001 gives it no way to reload a rule.

**How content reaches the database.** Seeding on first startup was rejected
because it makes the server something that writes its own rules, and because
"first startup" is a state that is easy to get wrong on a redeploy. Loading
entirely out of band was rejected because it would leave no supported path from
a written rule set to a running server. A load command the operator runs was
chosen.

## Consequences

**Rule sets gained a level.** A rule set is now written under the content it
checks — `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:` — because the two have different
fields and a flat namespace would leave `title` belonging to nothing in
particular. Existing rule set files must be re-indented under `testCase:`. The
loader refuses a rule set naming anything else, so a file that was not migrated
fails loudly rather than binding to nothing and never firing.

**The server no longer reads a file.** Rule sets are read from the database at
startup, which resolves the tension the README flagged against ADR-0001: there
is no mounted path any more. Reading once at startup and never reloading is
unchanged, and so is rule set version, which is still derived from the rule set
text exactly as supplied.

**There is one write path, and the server is not on it.** `npm run load` is the
only thing in the project that writes to the database. The object the server
holds exposes no write at all, so relaxing a rule or authoring a document is not
something the running system can do, whatever reaches it over HTTP.

**Rule sets are appended, not replaced.** Superseding a rule set does not destroy
the one a running server is still judging by, so an operator can read back,
compare or recover what was in force before a load. Nothing in the API resolves a
version to its row — reading one back is an operator with a database client, not
a feature — so this is history kept cheaply, not a lookup the server offers.

**A document's shape is taken from its file.** The file name without its
extension is the id a caller retrieves it by; the first line is the title,
written as a Markdown heading; the rest is the body. Every file in the directory
is read as a document — a file that is not one is refused by name rather than
skipped, because a document silently left out is one the agent will never know it
was meant to have. Names opening with a dot are the exception, being the
operating system's rather than the operator's.

**One report covers everything an operator supplied.** The load command checks
the rule sets and the documents before writing either, and reports their problems
together. A rule set problem must not hide a document problem, or the operator
loads twice to find both — the same bargain the server makes at startup when it
names every invalid rule at once.
=== 0006-rule-sets-and-documents-are-written-with-sql.md ===
# Rule Sets and Reference Documents are written with SQL, and the project ships no loader

An operator writes Rule Sets and Reference Documents into the database with SQL,
using whatever database client they already have. The project ships the schema
and stops there: there is no load command, nothing read off the filesystem, and
no template to copy. The server reads the database at startup exactly as before.

This reverses the "How content reaches the database" section of ADR-0005, which
chose a load command the operator runs. Everything else that ADR settled is
untouched — documents are still checked content held in the database, still
read-only over the API, still composed of a title and a body with their own Rule
Sets.

## Considered Options

**A load command reading files.** What ADR-0005 chose and what this replaces. Its
templates and its directory of documents were the thing that made the database
concrete while the schema was being designed; the maintainer's framing is that
they were a development intermediate whose job ended when the database became
real, and that keeping them means the project carries two representations of the
same Rule Sets for the rest of its life.

**A write surface on the server, kept off the agent's API.** Rejected. It is the
most usable answer for an operator without a database client, but it puts a write
path on the process ADR-0001 exists to keep off one, and defends the property by
network reachability rather than by the server holding an object that cannot
write. The weaker guarantee was not worth the convenience.

**Writing with SQL, out of band.** Chosen by the maintainer. ADR-0005 rejected
this on the grounds that it leaves no supported path from a written Rule Set to a
running server. That objection is answered rather than dismissed: the schema
ships in the repository as `schema.sql`, the README documents the statements that
write a Rule Set and a Reference Document, and the suite extracts and runs those
statements against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
tested. The path is supported; it is simply not automated.

ADR-0005's other objection, to seeding on first startup, is not answered because
it no longer applies: nothing seeds. The server gained no write, and "first
startup" is not a state anything here behaves differently in.

## Consequences

**The project no longer writes to its own database, at all.** ADR-0005 recorded
"there is one write path, and the server is not on it". There is now no write
path in the project. What ADR-0001 protects is stronger for it, not weaker: the
agent cannot relax a Rule that keeps rejecting it, and neither can anything this
repository ships.

**YAML stays, as the storage format.** Rule Sets are held as text in
`rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup, which is what the load command already
wrote and what the server already read. Removing the loader does not remove
YAML — an operator writes YAML inside a SQL statement — so the Rule Set
vocabulary, its checking, and the Rule Set Version derived from the text as
supplied are all unchanged.

**A Reference Document's shape is no longer taken from a file.** Its id, and its
two Fields, were read out of a file name and a Markdown heading; an operator now
writes all three directly. The Rules that reach a document are unchanged, and so
is what a read reports. What goes is the file convention and the refusal of a
file that is not a document.

**Applying the schema becomes an operator's step.** The load command created the
tables on first use. A fresh database now has none until `schema.sql` is applied,
so the server's refusal to start has to name that step rather than a command that
no longer exists. A database with no schema is still told apart from a database
that is unreachable, exactly as before.

**Nothing checks what an operator wrote before the server binds it.** The load
command validated Rule Sets and documents together and reported every problem in
one pass. Startup still refuses invalid Rule Sets and still reports every problem
at once, so that check survives — it happens when the server starts rather than
when the Rule Set is written. A malformed Reference Document is no longer refused
at all: its Fields are whatever the operator wrote.
=== 0007-a-rule-is-a-row-and-is-disabled-rather-than-deleted.md ===
# A Rule is a row, and is disabled rather than deleted

Rule Sets stop being one YAML document held as text and become rows, one per
Rule. A Rule carries the content and the Field it binds to, which kind of check
it is, what it looks for, the reason it gives, and a switch. An operator adds one
Rule, or turns one off, with a single statement naming that Rule alone.

Nothing is deleted. A Rule that should stop firing is disabled, and its row
stays. What a Rule looks for is not edited either — the reason it gives is. Both
are a discipline the schema documents and does not enforce, which is a decision
rather than an omission: there is one operator, and a guard's value is entirely
in who it stops.

This changes only how Rule Sets are stored and edited. They are still read once
at startup and never reloaded (ADR-0004), still written by an operator with SQL
with nothing in the project writing (ADR-0006), and a Rule still binds to exactly
one Field of one kind of content.

## Considered Options

**One YAML document, appended.** What this replaces. Its virtue is that the Rule
Set Version falls straight out of the bytes, and that a superseded document stays
readable because a new one is inserted beside it rather than over it. Its cost is
that every edit is an edit to the whole thing: turning off one Rule means
retyping every other Rule into a fresh `insert`, and a Rule Set of sixty Rules is
a wall of text where a one-character slip in an unrelated Rule is invisible. The
maintainer's framing is that a Rule Set is a list of independent checks and
should be edited as one.

**Rows, deleted when no longer wanted.** The obvious shape, and rejected. Every
response names the Rule Set Version and every Violation is logged against it, so
the system has already promised to explain a rejection after the fact. A deleted
Rule breaks that promise silently: the log still names the Rule, and the Rule is
not there to be read. The test cases rejected by it stay rejected and become
unexplainable, which lands on the QA engineer who wrote them rather than on the
operator who deleted the Rule. Delete also buys very little — a disabled Rule
stops firing exactly as completely as a deleted one, so what is saved is table
size, at a scale (tens of rows) no database notices.

**Rows, disabled rather than deleted.** Chosen. `enabled` is both the switch and
the tombstone, so the operator has three operations rather than four and the
record of what once fired survives. Turning a Rule back on is one statement and
restores the exact Rule that was there, rather than a retyped approximation of
it.

**A table per kind — one for Terms, one for Symbols.** Considered because the
columns differ: a Symbol carries Flanking and a Term does not. Rejected. A
Field's Rule Set is one list that mixes both, so two tables means every read is a
union and every operation an operator performs has to start by working out which
table the Rule is in. One table with a column naming the kind keeps the statement
shapes identical.

## Consequences

**The Rule Set Version is derived from the Rules in force, not from text.** It
was a hash of the YAML exactly as supplied; there is no longer a document to
hash. It becomes a hash over the enabled Rules, rendered in a fixed order and
including everything a caller was judged by — the Field, the kind, what is looked
for, the Flanking, the reason, and the Exceptions. Disabled Rules are left out,
because they judge nothing.

What the version is for is unchanged: it names the Rules a response was produced
by, and it cannot go on naming Rules that have since been edited. One property
improves. Because the version comes from the Rules rather than from their
formatting, the same Rules always produce the same version — so a Rule disabled
and later enabled again returns the Rule Set to the version it had before, rather
than to a new one that means the same thing. Under the old scheme, reformatting
the YAML changed the version without changing a Rule; that no longer happens, and
the safety argument for it no longer applies, because there is no formatting left
to change.

**What a Rule looks for cannot be edited; what it says can.** Changing `looks_for`
or the kind of check makes it a different check under the same name, and every
Violation already logged against that name then describes something that never
happened. Changing the reason changes only the wording the caller is handed.
Rewording a reason changes the Rule Set Version, which is correct: what a caller
is told is part of what the Rules do.

An operator who wants a Rule to look for something else disables it and adds
another, which is the honest shape of that change anyway.

**The discipline is not enforced, and that is decided rather than left open.**
Everywhere else, this project has made the unwanted thing impossible rather than
forbidden — the server holds an object with no write (ADR-0006), the agent has no
reload endpoint (ADR-0004). This is the exception, and it is worth naming as one.

The enforcing move exists: a trigger refusing a `delete` on `rules`, and refusing
an update that touches the identity columns, naming what to do instead. Postgres
takes it. What it cannot do is live in `schema.sql`, because the suite runs the
shipped schema against pg-mem, and pg-mem cannot parse
`create function ... language plpgsql` — adding the trigger makes the schema
unrunnable there and fails thirteen tests. So enforcing it means either giving
the suite a real Postgres, or shipping the trigger in a second file the suite
does not run.

**Chosen by the maintainer: neither. The discipline stays a discipline**, written
in the schema's comments and in this ADR, with nothing stopping a `delete`.

The reason is the whole of it: **there is one operator, and it is the maintainer.**
A guard's value is entirely in who it stops. It stops the person who does not know
the rule, or who has forgotten it — and here there is no such person. Paying for a
wall against yourself, today, is paying for nothing. The other two options were
priced at roughly thirty-five lines and one afternoon, and at a test suite that
must start a real database; neither is expensive, and both buy the same nothing
while the operator count is one.

An API in front of the database was raised and rejected on the merits, twice over.
It would give this project the write path ADR-0001 and ADR-0006 exist to remove,
and it would not even work: the operator writes SQL directly, so they are already
past any door an API could guard.

**What makes this reversible, and what the trigger would be.** The day a second
person writes SQL against this database, the calculation changes and this should
be revisited. The upgrade is small and does not disturb anything here: a
`schema-guards.sql` carrying the trigger, applied once, plus a startup check
asking whether the guard is installed and refusing to start when it is not. That
check is a read, so the server gains no write and ADR-0006 is untouched. It is
recorded here so the option does not have to be rediscovered.

**What is accepted in the meantime.** `delete from rules` works. A Rule deleted
that way takes with it the ability to explain every Violation already logged
against it, and nothing warns anyone at the time.

**What the constraints do cover is tested.** A Field that does not belong to its
content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is more than
one character, an empty reason, a duplicate Rule name on one Field, an Exception
pointing at no Rule — every one of those is refused by the schema as shipped, and
pg-mem enforces all of them. One character is written `looks_for like '_'` rather
than with a length function: it counts characters rather than bytes, which is the
same reading the server makes, and pg-mem has no length function to call.

**Exceptions are rows too, and follow the same discipline.** An Exception belongs
to exactly one Rule, as it always has. Removing one makes its Rule fire where it
previously did not, which is a change to what the Rules do, so an Exception is
disabled rather than deleted for the same reason a Rule is.

**The operator no longer writes YAML.** Rule Sets were YAML held in a text
column, written inside a SQL string with its apostrophes doubled. They are now
ordinary columns. What goes with the YAML is its parser at startup, its parse
error reporting, and the nesting that bound a Rule to a Field — the binding is
now two columns.

**Some checking moves into the database.** A Field that does not belong to the
content, a Flanking value that is not `whitespace`, a Symbol that is not one
character, an empty reason: these were startup refusals and become constraints,
so they are refused when the operator writes them rather than when the server
next starts. That is the better moment — the operator is present. Startup still
refuses a Rule Set it cannot bind, because a constraint cannot express everything
and a database restored from elsewhere is not something the schema witnessed.

**Nothing in `src/` reads this yet.** This ADR and the schema record the design.
The server still reads `rule_sets` and parses YAML, so applying the new schema
alone leaves a server that starts against the old table. Wiring it up is separate
work, and until it is done the two coexist.

> Done in #26. The server reads `rules` and `rule_exceptions`, `rule_sets` is
> gone from the schema, and the YAML parser and its dependency went with it.

**`CONTEXT.md` needs its Rule Set Version entry rewritten.** It currently says
the version is derived from the rule sets as supplied and names the text rather
than the Rules parsed out of it. Both halves are now wrong.

> Done in #21. The entry describes the Rules in force, and #26 adds the rule id
> to what it says the version covers — a Rule renamed is a Rule a caller reads
> differently, so a version that ignored the id would name two Rule Sets as one.
=== 0008-a-default-set-of-rules-ships-as-sql-the-operator-applies.md ===
# A default set of Rules ships as SQL the operator applies

`default-rules.sql` ships in the repository beside `schema.sql`, and is applied
the same way and by the same hand. It writes 89 checks — 74 Terms and 15
Symbols, for the tells that a piece of writing came from a model — against each
of the five Fields, so 445 Rules arrive, all enabled.

Nothing about the write path changes. The operator applies it, the server reads
what is there at startup, and this project still writes nothing to its own
database (ADR-0006). A Rule is still a row and is still switched off rather than
deleted (ADR-0007), which is how this file is meant to be tuned.

## The ADR-0006 line this sits against

ADR-0006 says the project "ships the schema and stops there: there is no load
command, nothing read off the filesystem, and **no template to copy**." A file of
default Rules is close enough to that last clause to be worth answering rather
than stepping around.

What that clause was rejecting was the loader's templates: files the project read
at runtime, which had to stay in step with the database and gave the project two
representations of the same Rule Sets for the rest of its life. None of that
applies here. Nothing reads `default-rules.sql` at runtime — `grep` finds it in
no source file, no script and no compose service. It is not a second
representation of Rules the database also holds; it is the statements that put
them there once, in the same position `schema.sql` occupies. After it is applied
the database is the only representation, and an operator who tunes a Rule tunes
the row, never the file.

The property ADR-0006 exists to protect is untouched: the generating agent cannot
loosen a Rule that keeps rejecting it (ADR-0001), and neither can anything this
repository ships.

## Considered Options

**A SQL file the operator applies.** Chosen by the maintainer. It costs the
operator one command they are already taking a version of, and the suite runs the
shipped file against an in-process Postgres, so what is documented is what is
tested — the same standard ADR-0006 set for the README's statements.

**The server seeds an empty `rules` table.** Rejected. It is the only option that
is default without the operator doing anything, and it is bought by giving the
server a write path into its own Rules, which reverses ADR-0006 and weakens
ADR-0001 to no purpose. The convenience is one command.

**The tables as README documentation only.** Rejected. Cheapest, and it drifts:
nothing runs it, so nothing catches a Rule that the schema would refuse. Six of
the eighty-nine carry an apostrophe and one is a character that must be a single
code point; none of that survives being retyped out of a table by hand.

**Every Rule shipped disabled.** Considered seriously, and rejected by the
maintainer. It answers the trimming problem directly — nobody decides up front
whether `ensure that` is too noisy, and the operator switches on what earns its
place. It was rejected because a file that does nothing when applied is a file
whose effect is never seen, and because the honest way to learn which Rules are
too noisy is to have them reject something.

## Consequences

**Applying it will reject Test Cases a tester wrote by hand.** This is the known
cost of shipping enabled and untrimmed. `ensure that`, `correctly`, `properly`
and `various` are ordinary QA English, and the QA-specific block is named in the
file as the rows to switch off first. The file is a starting point to tune down,
not a setting to accept.

**The Rules are not this project's opinions.** Every row traces to one of six
published anti-AI-writing references, named in the file's header and read in
`docs/sessions/2026-08-14-anti-ai-writing-rule-tables.md`. Where the references
disagree with the row, the file says so: `no-spaced-semicolon` and
`no-spaced-colon` are recorded in it as catching odd spacing and **not** catching
an AI tell, because the 2026 measurements say models use fewer semicolons than
people do, and a Rule firing on one penalises the human habit. They ship because
they cost nothing, and the file refuses to pretend they are more than that.

**Applying it twice is safe, and does not undo tuning.** Each statement carries
`on conflict (content_kind, field, rule_id) do nothing`, so a Rule already there
is left exactly as it is. An operator who has switched Rules off can re-apply the
file without switching them back on — which matters, because a second `psql -f`
silently pulling back the operator's only lever would make that lever untrustable.

**What the two tables cannot reach is written down in the file.** The full
"it is not X, it is Y" frame, the rule of three, any threshold, thin punctuation,
uniform sentence length, Title Case and the bold-header bullet layout are all out
of reach of a Term and a Symbol. They are listed in the file so an absent Rule is
not read as a clean area. Closing the first of them needs a third kind of check,
with holes in it, and nothing here is blocked on that.

**A Term is literal, so an apostrophe is two Rules' worth of coverage.** The six
Terms carrying one hold a straight apostrophe, and the same phrase written with a
curly one does not match them. It is still caught, by `no-curly-apostrophe` firing
on the character, but under that Rule and with that reason.

# Domain Docs

How the engineering skills should consume this repo's domain documentation when exploring the codebase.

This is a **single-context** repo: one `CONTEXT.md` and one `docs/adr/`, both at the root.

## Before exploring, read these

- **`CONTEXT.md`** at the repo root — the project's vocabulary.
- **`docs/adr/`** — read the ADRs that touch the area you're about to work in.

If any of these files don't exist, **proceed silently**. Don't flag their absence; don't suggest creating them upfront. The `/domain-modeling` skill (reached via `/grill-with-docs` and `/improve-codebase-architecture`) creates them lazily when terms or decisions actually get resolved.

## File structure

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/adr/
│   ├── 0001-validation-is-outside-the-agent-trust-boundary.md
│   ├── 0002-detection-is-deterministic.md
│   └── 0003-agent-works-only-over-the-api.md
└── README.md
```

There is no source tree yet — the project is design-only at this point. When one appears, it sits alongside these files; the docs stay at the root.

## Use the glossary's vocabulary

When your output names a domain concept (in an issue title, a refactor proposal, a hypothesis, a test name), use the term as defined in `CONTEXT.md`. Don't drift to synonyms the glossary explicitly avoids.

If the concept you need isn't in the glossary yet, that's a signal — either you're inventing language the project doesn't use (reconsider) or there's a real gap (note it for `/domain-modeling`).

## Flag ADR conflicts

If your output contradicts an existing ADR, surface it explicitly rather than silently overriding:

> _Contradicts ADR-0002 (detection is deterministic) — but worth reopening because…_

## STUDY PAYLOAD — /home/jack/src/testcase-validator

Method run in order: ground truth (src/, package.json, schema.sql, default-rules.sql, docker-compose.yml, .env.example, .mcp.json*, tsconfig.json) → organizing idea → key points → absorption check → diagrams → docs pass last.

**Constraints held (all seven):** (1) I wrote no file anywhere — no Write/Edit, no redirection, no mkdir/touch; this list exists only in this reply. (2) The target repo was read only — no git state change, no writes. (3) README.md / CONTEXT.md / CLAUDE.md / docs/ stayed shut until step 5, after the model was derived from code. (4) I ran no test command — no vitest, npm test, npx. (5) No docker/podman command of any kind. (6) No test file was read and no key point comes from a test name; I note only that `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/test/` exists (24 files) and that there is **no `.github/` and no CI workflow at all** in the repo. (7) No issue, design doc, draft, session log or skill file read — `docs/sessions/*` was deliberately left unopened even in step 5.

**Absorption question (step 4):** on the first pass, **yes** — "a read is never refused, content plus violations" was living only inside #1's mechanism, and #1 must carry no other key point's mechanism. It was promoted, taking the list to five, and I take step 3's stated route: **five, stated as five**, because nothing on the list could be demoted without losing a behaviour tests are measured against (I checked the two demotion candidates: the TestLink absence-vs-outage classification is genuinely stage three of #3's mechanism, and Exceptions are genuinely inside #5's mechanism, so neither forced a sixth). Asked again over the settled five: **no** — no remaining behaviour is explained only inside another key point's mechanism.

**Count check: 5 diagrams drawn == 5 key points. PASS.**

---

### #1 — Organizing idea

**Key point:** Every route to TestLink runs through this one Fastify process, and the two things the generating agent must not be able to touch — the TestLink credentials and the Rules — are held on the far side of it: the agent speaks HTTP and nothing else, the operator speaks SQL and nothing else, and no code path in `src/` writes to the database.

**Ground truth:** `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/stdio-tool-caller.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/tool-caller.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/docker-compose.yml`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/.env.example`

**Mechanism:** `server.ts` builds `new PostgresStore(await connectToPostgres(required('DATABASE_URL')))`; `PostgresStore` implements `DocumentStore` and exposes exactly three methods — `rules()`, `listDocuments()`, `getDocument(id)` — all `select`, no `insert`/`update`/`delete` anywhere in `src/`. It reads `required('TESTLINK_URL')`, `required('TESTLINK_API_KEY')`, `required('TESTLINK_AUTHOR_LOGIN')` from its own env and spawns testlink-mcp itself via `connectToTestLinkMcp` (`StdioClientTransport`), default `docker run --rm -i -e TESTLINK_URL -e TESTLINK_API_KEY dogkeeper886/testlink-mcp:${expectedTestLinkMcp}` where `expectedTestLinkMcp = '1.6.0'` lives in `mcp-testlink-client.ts`; `TESTLINK_MCP_COMMAND` + `TESTLINK_MCP_ARGS` (JSON list) override for a source checkout. `buildApp({testlink, documents, rules, logger})` mounts the whole HTTP surface: `/projects` (GET/POST), `/projects/:projectId` (PUT/DELETE), `/projects/:projectId/suites` (GET/POST), `/projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId` (PUT/DELETE), `/projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases` (GET/POST), `/test-cases/:id` (GET/PUT/DELETE), `/reference-documents` (GET), `/reference-documents/:id` (GET). There is no rule route, no reload route, no document write route, no validate-only route. Two Postgres instances exist in compose: `validator-db` (postgres:17, published on 5433) holding `rules`/`rule_exceptions`/`reference_documents`, and `db` (postgres:9.6) which is TestLink's own.

**Why it matters:** a newcomer who reads this as "an API in front of TestLink" will look for the place that seeds or edits Rules and never find it, and will not understand why `DocumentStore` has no `putDocument`. The shape of the whole project is: the agent is the untrusted party, so anything the agent could use to loosen a check is deliberately unreachable from the process the agent talks to.

**Diagram:**
```
 generating agent                      operator, out of band
        |  HTTP only                          |  psql / SQL only
        v                                     v
+--------------------------------+    +---------------------------+
| testcase-validator (Fastify)   |    | validator-db  pg17 :5433  |
|  server.ts -> buildApp()       |    |   rules                   |
|   /test-cases  /projects       |<---+   rule_exceptions         |
|   /projects/:p/suites          | rd |   reference_documents     |
|   /reference-documents  (GET)  |    +---------------------------+
|  holds TESTLINK_API_KEY        |     PostgresStore = rules() +
|  no write route, no reload     |     listDocuments() + getDocument()
+---------------+----------------+     ...and nothing that writes
                | ToolCaller.call(tool, args)   [MCP over stdio]
                v
   docker run --rm -i dogkeeper886/testlink-mcp:1.6.0   (pinned)
                | XML-RPC
                v
            TestLink (testlink-code fork, compose :8090)
```

**Contradicts:** `docs/adr/0001-...md` still states "Rules are baked into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted path" — the code reads them from Postgres at startup; ADR-0004 openly records this ("ADR-0001 no longer describes the store accurately"), so the ADR set knows, but the 0001 text itself is untrue as written. `docs/agents/domain.md` states "There is no source tree yet — the project is design-only at this point" and lists only ADRs 0001–0003; `src/` holds twelve modules and there are eight ADRs.

---

### #2 — Rules are frozen at startup, or the server does not start

**Key point:** The Rules are read from the database exactly once, before the server listens; zero enabled Rules or any malformed row aborts startup with every problem named at once, and the sha256 of the Rules that survived becomes the `Rule-Set-Version` stamped on every single reply for the life of the process.

**Ground truth:** `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`

**Mechanism:** `PostgresStore.rules()` first calls `hasSchema(queries)` — `select 1 from information_schema.tables where table_name = 'rules'` — so a database the schema was never applied to answers `[]` rather than throwing; then `select id, rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, flanked, reason from rules where enabled order by id`, plus a separate `select rule, phrase from rule_exceptions where enabled order by id` gathered by `exceptionsByRule` into `Map<number, string[]>` (separate statement, deliberately not a join). `server.ts` throws `'No enabled Rules are in the database, so the server will not start...'` when `rules.length === 0`. Inside `buildApp`, `bindRules(rules)` → `checkRules` → `checkStoredRule` per row, which re-checks in code every constraint `schema.sql` already declares (`rule_id <> ''`, `content_kind in ('testCase','referenceDocument')`, `field_belongs_to_the_content`, `a_symbol_is_one_character` via `[...looksFor].length !== 1`, `only_a_symbol_is_flanked`, `reason <> ''`); every failure is pushed to `problems` and `refuse(problems)` throws one message listing all of them. `ruleSetVersionOf(rules)` JSON-stringifies `[contentKind, field, ruleId, category, looksFor, flanked, reason, exceptions.sort()]` per Rule, sorts the strings, joins with `\n`, sha256, `.slice(0,12)` — the row `id` and the database's ordering are deliberately excluded, so disabling and re-enabling a Rule returns the version to its previous value. An `onSend` hook sets `Rule-Set-Version` on every reply including the 204 from a delete; `versioned(body)` adds `ruleSetVersion` to the body only where Rules judged the content.

**Why it matters:** nothing in this system reloads. A newcomer who edits a row and expects it to take effect, or who looks for the place the version is declared, is looking for machinery that does not exist — and the reason it does not exist is #1's boundary: a reload path is a path the agent could drive.

**Diagram:**
```
server.ts
  connectToPostgres(DATABASE_URL)
        v
  PostgresStore.rules()
    hasSchema()? --no--> []      (fresh db = "no Rules", not an outage)
        | yes
        v  select ... from rules where enabled order by id
           select rule,phrase from rule_exceptions where enabled
        v
  rules.length === 0 --> throw "No enabled Rules ... will not start"
        v
  buildApp({rules})
    bindRules -> checkRules -> checkStoredRule per row
        |   any problem -> refuse(): ONE throw listing EVERY problem
        v
    ruleSetVersionOf = sha256(sort(JSON tuples)).slice(0,12)   e.g. 9f3ac1d0b2e7
        |          (no row id, no db order, disabled Rules excluded)
        v
    onSend hook -> header Rule-Set-Version on EVERY reply (204 included)
        v
  app.listen({ port: PORT ?? 3000, host: '0.0.0.0' })
```

**Contradicts:** `docs/adr/0006-...md` still says "**YAML stays, as the storage format.** Rule Sets are held as text in `rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup" — there is no `rule_sets` table in `schema.sql`, no YAML parser in `src/`, and no yaml dependency in `package.json`; ADR-0006 carries no superseded banner (ADR-0007 records the change, with a `> Done in #26` note, but 0006 was never annotated). `README.md` ("Decided") says "Rule sets are appended rather than replaced… nothing in the API resolves a version back to its row" and "A rule set is written under the content it checks, `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:`" — both are YAML/rule-set-row era: a Rule Set is not stored at all (`CONTEXT.md` says so itself), there is no rule-set row and no version column, and the content kind is a column value `'testCase'`, not a YAML key with a colon. Same stale claim repeats in `docs/adr/0005-...md` ("Rule sets are appended, not replaced", "Rule sets gained a level… Existing rule set files must be re-indented under `testCase:`", "The loader refuses a rule set naming anything else") — 0005's banner disclaims only its "How content reaches the database" section and one consequence, so these remain as unretracted claims about a loader that does not exist (`package.json` has only `dev`, `typecheck`, `test`; `npm run load` from ADR-0005 would fail).

---

### #3 — A write refuses in three stages, and each refusal is a different answer

**Key point:** A submitted or updated Test Case can be turned away at exactly three places — the JSON Schema (400, `refusal:'schema'`, no violations, no version in body), the Rules (422 with every Violation and the version, nothing written), and the TestLink call itself (404 absent / 409 unconfirmed prefix / throw→500 outage) — and the three are told apart by shape, never by parsing an error string.

**Ground truth:** `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/tool-caller.ts`

**Mechanism:** Fastify is built with `ajv: { customOptions: { coerceTypes: false } }`; `testCaseSchema` (`required: ['name','summary']`, `additionalProperties: false`) is attached to POST `/projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases` and PUT `/test-cases/:id`, and `setErrorHandler` turns `error.validation` into `reply.code(400).send({ refusal:'schema', message })` — no `versioned()`. Stage two: `findViolations(request.body, bound.testCase)`; if non-empty, `reject()` emits one `request.log.warn({ruleSetVersion, field, rule}, 'Rule violated')` per Violation and returns `reply.code(422).send(versioned({ violations }))` — the TestLink client is never called. Stage three is `McpTestLinkClient.answer(tool, args, alsoTheCallers?)`: `tools.call` returns `{text, isError}`; `isError`, or a body whose first record carries `code` + string `message` (`reportedProblem`), goes to `place()`, which checks in order `alsoTheCallers` (`reportsUnconfirmed = /Confirmation failed/i` → `unconfirmed` symbol → route answers 409), `reportsMissingTool = /Unknown tool/i` → throw naming `1.6.0`, `reportsAbsence = /does not exist|not found/i` → `absent` symbol → route answers `nothingThere()` 404, and **anything unmatched throws** → 500. A successful-looking body whose first record has `status === false` (`deniedIn`) also throws, and `idOf` throws when TestLink names no id (or `0`/`''`) for a create. Absence is read only from what TestLink reported about the call, never from served content. Codes on success: POST 201 `versioned({id})`, PUT 200 `versioned({id})`, DELETE 204 (header only).

**Why it matters:** four distinct client-visible outcomes share one HTTP surface, and the entire design turns on their being distinguishable by an agent reading the body: a 422 means rewrite the wording, a 404 means fix the id, a 409 means restate the prefix, a 500 means retry later. Anyone who collapses "TestLink said no" into one code destroys the contract.

**Diagram:**
```
POST /projects/:p/suites/:s/test-cases   body {name, summary, preconditions?}
 |
 |-(1) ajv testCaseSchema, coerceTypes:false, additionalProperties:false
 |      fail -> 400 {refusal:'schema', message}
 |             no violations, no ruleSetVersion in body (header still set)
 v pass
 |-(2) findViolations(body, bound.testCase)
 |      any  -> log.warn per Violation -> 422 {violations[], ruleSetVersion}
 |              nothing reaches TestLink
 v none
 |-(3) McpTestLinkClient.createTestCase -> tools.call('create_test_case')
 |      place(message) in order:
 |        /Confirmation failed/i -> unconfirmed -> 409  (delete_project)
 |        /Unknown tool/i        -> throw "older than 1.6.0"
 |        /does not exist|not found/i -> absent -> 404 nothingThere()
 |        anything else          -> throw -> 500  (outage)
 |        status===false / no id -> throw -> 500
 v ok
 201 {id, ruleSetVersion}          PUT -> 200   DELETE -> 204 (header only)
```

**Contradicts:** none. (`README.md` "Decided" describes 400/404/409/500 and the header-without-body rule exactly as the code behaves.)

---

### #4 — A read is never refused; violations ride beside the content

**Key point:** `GET /test-cases/:id` and `GET /reference-documents/:id` run the very same Rules over what they serve and answer 200 with the stored content unchanged plus a `violations` array — no number of Violations can turn a read into a refusal, and 404 on a read means "nothing held under that id", not "rejected".

**Ground truth:** `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`

**Mechanism:** `GET /test-cases/:id` → `testlink.getTestCase(id)`; `McpTestLinkClient.getTestCase` calls `read_test_case`, takes `first(held)` (TestLink answers with versions) and projects exactly three fields through `text()` — `name`, `summary`, `preconditions`, empty string where TestLink holds nothing — so a TestLink record becomes a `TestCase`. Then `reply.send(versioned({ testCase, violations: findViolations(testCase, bound.testCase) }))`. `GET /reference-documents/:id` → `documents.getDocument(id)` → `select title, body from reference_documents where id = $1` (parameterised, so a caller-supplied id is data and never SQL) → `reply.send(versioned({ document, violations: findViolations(document, bound.referenceDocument) }))`; missing id → `404 {message: 'There is no Reference Document <id>.'}` with no `violations` key at all, so it cannot be misread as a Rejection. `GET /reference-documents` lists `{id, title}` only — bodies withheld. `bound.referenceDocument` is a separate `Map` from `bound.testCase` (`RuleSets = { testCase, referenceDocument }`), and `schema.sql`'s `field_belongs_to_the_content` CHECK plus `checkStoredRule` keep a Rule written for one from ever reaching the other. No logging on reads. `/projects` and `/suites` responses are served straight through with no `versioned()` and no violations — no Rule binds to them.

**Why it matters:** this is the only channel by which the agent sees existing content, so it is the exact place a legacy AI-writing fingerprint would be copied forward into a new Test Case. Reporting-without-refusing is the whole point; a newcomer who "fixes" the read path to reject bad content puts the content the caller most needs to see out of reach.

**Diagram:**
```
GET /test-cases/:id                    GET /reference-documents/:id
  testlink.getTestCase(id)               documents.getDocument(id)
   read_test_case -> first(version)       select title,body ... where id=$1
   -> {name, summary, preconditions}
    |                                      |
    | undefined -> 404 nothingThere        | undefined -> 404 {message}
    |    (no violations key)               |    (no violations key)
    v                                      v
  findViolations(testCase,               findViolations(document,
                 bound.testCase)                    bound.referenceDocument)
    v                                      v
  200 {testCase, violations[],           200 {document, violations[],
       ruleSetVersion}                         ruleSetVersion}

  stored content served UNCHANGED; violations sit beside it, never merged.
  No violation count ever downgrades a 200.   Reads log nothing.
```

**Contradicts:** none.

---

### #5 — Detection: Term as a word, Symbol as a character, Exceptions by span

**Key point:** Every Violation comes from literal matching with no model in the path — a Term matches its words in any casing, however they are spaced, but only standing as a word; a Symbol matches one character anywhere, or only whitespace-flanked; and each Rule is suppressed only where *its own* Exception phrase covers the whole match, with the field's every Rule reported in one pass.

**Ground truth:** `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/default-rules.sql`

**Mechanism:** `findViolations(content, ruleSets)` iterates the `Map<field, RuleSet>`, skips a field whose value is `undefined`, and runs every Rule bound to it, so a caller sees all problems at once. `termViolations` uses `matcherFor(term)`: regex-escape, then `replace(/\s+/g, '\\s+')`, flags `giu` — so `in today's` matches across a line break and in any casing — and keeps a hit only when `standsAsWord`, i.e. both neighbours satisfy `isOutsideAWord` = `character === undefined || !/[\p{L}\p{N}_-]/u.test(character)`; a word therefore runs through `-` and `_`, so `utilise` leaves `utilises` and `re-associates` alone. `symbolViolations` walks `indexOf` and, when `flanked === 'whitespace'`, requires `isGap` on both sides where the edge of the field counts as whitespace. Suppression: `suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)` uses the same `spansOf` matcher but with **no** word-standing check, so an Exception matches inside a longer word; `isSuppressed` keeps a Violation unless `offset >= span.start && offset + text.length <= span.end`. The emitted `Violation` is `{field, rule: rule.id, reason, text (as found, in the casing found), offset}` — deliberately no suggested replacement. `default-rules.sql` supplies 74 Terms × 5 fields + 15 Symbols × 5 fields (verified by count: 74 and 15) = 445 rows, inserted by cross-join with `on conflict (content_kind, field, rule_id) do nothing`, and its own trailing comment names what this vocabulary cannot express: the full "not X, it is Y" frame, the rule of three, any threshold (a Rule fires per occurrence; nothing counts), thin punctuation, uniform sentence length, Title Case, and bold-header bullet layout.

**Why it matters:** this is where "validation" actually happens, and it is much narrower than the word suggests. A newcomer who does not know that a Term is word-standing but an Exception is not, or that nothing in the system counts anything, will both misread false negatives as bugs and expect thresholds the design has no room for.

**Diagram:**
```
findViolations(content, ruleSets)        ruleSets: Map<field, Rule[]>
  per field in the Map (a field no Rule names is simply absent)
    value = content[field]      undefined -> skip
      per rule bound to that field
         type 'term'                    type 'symbol'
         matcherFor(): escape, \s+      indexOf(symbol) loop
           between words, flags /giu    flanked==='whitespace' ?
         standsAsWord(): both sides       isGap(prev) && isGap(next)
           outside /[\p{L}\p{N}_-]/u      (edge of field = whitespace)
              |                                 |
              +----------------+----------------+
                               v
        suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)   <- THIS Rule's own
           same matcher, NO word-standing check      Exceptions only
                               v
        isSuppressed: offset >= start && offset+len <= end
                               v
        Violation {field, rule:id, reason, text(as found), offset}
                    no suggested replacement, nothing counted
```

**Contradicts:** none. `README.md`'s counts check out exactly — 74 Terms, 15 Symbols, 89 checks, 445 Rules across five fields.

---

## Doc-vs-code contradictions found (step 5, consolidated)

1. **`docs/adr/0006` — `rule_sets.source` and YAML.** Claims Rule Sets are held as YAML text in a `rule_sets` table parsed at startup. That table does not exist in `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, no parser exists in `src/`, and `package.json` has no yaml dependency. ADR-0006 carries no superseded note (ADR-0007 does the superseding and annotates only itself).
2. **`docs/adr/0005` — the loader.** Its banner retracts only the "How content reaches the database" section; the surviving consequences still describe `npm run load` writing to the database, a loader refusing a mis-nested rule set, rule sets re-indented under `testCase:`, and a document's id/title/body read out of a file name and a Markdown heading. `package.json` ships only `dev`, `typecheck`, `test` — `npm run load` fails; nothing reads the filesystem.
3. **`docs/adr/0001` — "baked into the deployed image".** Untrue of the code (Rules come from Postgres). ADR-0004 records the drift explicitly, so this is a known-but-uncorrected claim rather than a hidden one.
4. **`README.md` "Decided" — rule-set rows and YAML syntax.** "Rule sets are appended rather than replaced… nothing in the API resolves a version back to its row" describes rows that do not exist (a Rule Set is not stored — `CONTEXT.md` says so itself), and "written under the content it checks, `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:`" is YAML-key syntax for what is now the `content_kind` column value.
5. **`docs/agents/domain.md` — "There is no source tree yet — the project is design-only at this point."** `src/` holds twelve modules; its file-structure block also lists only ADRs 0001–0003 of eight.
6. **Documented default config cannot reach the documented TestLink.** `.env.example` and `README.md` set `TESTLINK_URL=http://localhost:8090` "the address the compose file publishes on", while `server.ts`'s default launch is `docker run --rm -i -e TESTLINK_URL -e TESTLINK_API_KEY dogkeeper886/testlink-mcp:1.6.0` with **no** `--network host` — inside that container `localhost:8090` is the container itself, not the host. The repo's own working `.mcp.json` (gitignored) does add `--network host`; `.mcp.json.example` sidesteps it with a public hostname. Following the README as written, the default path to TestLink does not connect.
7. Not verified, by constraint: `README.md`'s claims that "the suite extracts and runs" the documented SQL statements and that Vitest exercises "four seams" — these are claims about test files, which I did not read.

Everything else checked out: the `psql`/compose commands, ports (5433 validator-db, 8090 TestLink), `npm run dev`, the refusal-to-start wording, the `Rule-Set-Version` header-versus-body rule, `?confirmPrefix=`, the read-never-refused contract, the exception-by-three-columns SQL example, and the 74/15/89/445 counts.

content.text:
## Payload — analysis-sut study of `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator`

Steps 1–5 complete. Settled list is **five** key points (justification under the absorption answer at the end).

---

### #1 — Organizing idea

**Key point:** The validator is the *only* path from the generating agent to TestLink and to the Rules: the agent speaks HTTP and nothing else, while the server process alone holds `TESTLINK_API_KEY`, spawns `testlink-mcp` itself, and reaches Postgres through an object that has no write method — so no request of any shape can add, edit or reload a Rule or a Reference Document.

**Ground truth:**
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/stdio-tool-caller.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/default-rules.sql`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/docker-compose.yml`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/.env.example`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/package.json`

**Mechanism:** `server.ts` calls `required('DATABASE_URL')` → `connectToPostgres` → `new PostgresStore(queries)`. `PostgresStore` implements `DocumentStore` and exposes exactly three reads — `rules()`, `listDocuments()`, `getDocument(id)` — and no write anywhere in `src/`. It then calls `connectToTestLinkMcp({...testLinkMcp(), env: {TESTLINK_URL, TESTLINK_API_KEY}})`, which spawns `docker run --rm -i -e TESTLINK_URL -e TESTLINK_API_KEY dogkeeper886/testlink-mcp:${expectedTestLinkMcp}` (`expectedTestLinkMcp = '1.6.0'`, pinned in `src/mcp-testlink-client.ts`, overridable only by the operator's `TESTLINK_MCP_COMMAND` + JSON `TESTLINK_MCP_ARGS`). `buildApp({testlink: new McpTestLinkClient(tools, {authorLogin}), documents: store, rules, logger:{level:'warn'}})` returns the Fastify instance; `app.listen({port: PORT ?? 3000, host: '0.0.0.0'})`. Content reaches Postgres only by an operator running `psql -f schema.sql` and optionally `psql -f default-rules.sql`. `package.json` has three scripts: `dev`, `typecheck`, `test` — no loader, no migration runner, no seed.

**Why it matters:** A newcomer reading only the routes sees a CRUD proxy. The point of the project is the direction of the arrows: config, credentials and Rules all enter the process from the operator's side and none of them are reachable from the caller's side. Every other design choice (read-once Rules, no reload endpoint, read-only documents, SQL-only writes) is a consequence of this one and is unreadable without it.

**Diagram:**
```
 generating agent  (holds no API key, no DB credentials, no files)
        | HTTP only
        v
+--------------------- server.ts (one process) ---------------------+
| required('DATABASE_URL')        required('TESTLINK_URL',          |
|        |                                 'TESTLINK_API_KEY',      |
|        v                                 'TESTLINK_AUTHOR_LOGIN') |
| PostgresStore  (read only:               |                        |
|   rules / listDocuments / getDocument)   v                        |
|        |                        connectToTestLinkMcp (stdio)      |
|        |                        docker run testlink-mcp:1.6.0     |
|        +------> buildApp({testlink, documents, rules}) <----+     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
         |                                             |
         v                                             v
  postgres:17  rules / rule_exceptions /          TestLink (XML-RPC)
               reference_documents                dogkeeper886/
         ^                                        testlink-code fork
         | psql -f schema.sql, -f default-rules.sql
    operator only -- nothing in src/ writes here
```

**Contradicts:**
- `docs/adr/0006-...md` §"YAML stays, as the storage format": *"Rule Sets are held as text in `rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup."* No `rule_sets` table exists in `schema.sql`, no YAML parser exists in `src/`, and no YAML dependency exists in `package.json`. ADR-0006 carries no superseded banner; ADR-0007 records the change but 0006 still asserts it.
- `docs/adr/0005-...md` consequences beyond its banner: *"`npm run load` is the only thing in the project that writes to the database"* (no `load` script exists), *"The loader refuses a rule set naming anything else"* (no loader), *"A document's shape is taken from its file"* (`reference_documents` is written by the operator), *"One report covers everything an operator supplied"* (no load-time report). The banner disclaims only the "How content reaches the database" section and one consequence, so these remain live claims the code does not support.
- `docs/adr/0001-...md`: *"Rules are baked into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted path"* — Rules are rows read from Postgres at startup. (ADR-0004 flags this itself; recording it because ADR-0001 was not amended.)
- `docs/agents/domain.md`: *"There is no source tree yet — the project is design-only at this point."* `src/` holds 12 TypeScript files; its file-structure block also lists only ADRs 0001–0003 where eight exist.

---

### #2 — Rules are frozen at startup, or the server does not start

**Key point:** The Rules are read from the database exactly once, before the HTTP server exists; zero enabled Rules or any malformed row aborts startup with every problem named at once, and the `sha256` of the Rules that survived becomes a `Rule-Set-Version` stamped on every reply for the life of the process.

**Ground truth:**
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts` (lines 12–26)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts` (`checkStoredRule`, `checkRules`, `bindRules`, `refuse`, `ruleSetVersionOf`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts` (lines 146–171)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts` (`hasSchema`, `rules`, `exceptionsByRule`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`

**Mechanism:** `store.rules()` first asks `hasSchema` (`select 1 from information_schema.tables where table_name = 'rules'`) — a schema-less database answers `[]` rather than throwing, so "fresh database" is told from "unreachable database" without matching error text. It then selects `id, rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, flanked, reason from rules where enabled order by id`, and joins in `select rule, phrase from rule_exceptions where enabled order by id` as a second statement. `server.ts` throws `'No enabled Rules are in the database, so the server will not start…'` when the array is empty. `buildApp` calls `bindRules(rules)`, which runs `checkStoredRule` per row — empty `ruleId`, `contentKind` not in `{testCase, referenceDocument}`, a `field` not in `fieldNames[contentKind]`, empty `reason`, empty `term`, `flanked` on a term, a `symbol` whose `[...looksFor].length !== 1`, `flanked` not `'whitespace'`, unknown `category` — collects every failure into `problems`, and `refuse()` throws them all in one message. The same failures are also `check` constraints in `schema.sql` (`field_belongs_to_the_content`, `a_symbol_is_one_character`, `only_a_symbol_is_flanked`, `unique (content_kind, field, rule_id)`), so startup is the second line of defence for a database those constraints never saw. `ruleSetVersionOf` JSON-stringifies `[contentKind, field, ruleId, category, looksFor, flanked, reason, sorted exceptions]` per Rule, sorts the strings, joins with `\n`, sha256, `.slice(0,12)` — the row `id` and the database's ordering are deliberately excluded. `app.addHook('onSend')` sets the `Rule-Set-Version` header on every reply including the 204s; `versioned(body)` adds `ruleSetVersion` to the body only where Rules took part.

**Why it matters:** Nothing in this system re-reads a Rule. A newcomer who assumes a config reload, a per-request rule fetch, or a hot-swap will misread every subsequent behaviour — including why the version is a hash rather than an operator-typed string, and why a Rule switched off and back on returns the version to its previous value.

**Diagram:**
```
  hasSchema()? --no--> []
      |yes
      v
 select ... from rules where enabled order by id
 select rule, phrase from rule_exceptions where enabled
      |
      v
 rules.length === 0 --> throw 'No enabled Rules ... will not start'
      |
      v
 bindRules -> checkRules -> checkStoredRule(row) per row
      |                        |
      |                        +-> problem strings collected, never
      |                            thrown one at a time
      +-- problems.length > 0 --> refuse(): one throw, every problem
      |
      v
 RuleSets { testCase: Map<field,Rule[]>,
            referenceDocument: Map<field,Rule[]> }   <- fixed forever
      |
      v
 ruleSetVersionOf(rules) = sha256(sorted JSON tuples)[0..12)
      |
      +--> onSend hook: header Rule-Set-Version on EVERY reply
      +--> versioned(body): ruleSetVersion in body only where a
           Rule judged what was sent
```

**Contradicts:**
- `README.md` §Decided: *"Rule sets are appended rather than replaced, so superseding one does not destroy the one a running server is still judging by; nothing in the API resolves a version back to its row."* There is no rule-set row and no version column anywhere in `schema.sql` — a Rule Set is not stored at all (as `CONTEXT.md` itself says: *"Not a thing written down anywhere"*). The sentence describes the deleted `rule_sets` table.
- `README.md` §Decided: *"A rule set is written under the content it checks, `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:`"* — the trailing-colon form is YAML-era syntax; these are values of the `content_kind` column.
- `docs/adr/0007-...md`: *"Nothing in `src/` reads this yet… The server still reads `rule_sets` and parses YAML"* — false against the code, but the file carries an inline `> Done in #26` note, so it is annotated rather than stale.

---

### #3 — A write refuses in three stages, and each stage answers differently

**Key point:** A submitted Test Case can be turned away three times over and the caller can tell which from the response alone: `400 {refusal:'schema'}` before any Rule runs, `422 {violations, ruleSetVersion}` with nothing written, or a TestLink-stage answer — `404` for absent, `409` for an unconfirmed project delete, a throw (500) for anything the client cannot place.

**Ground truth:**
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts` (`testCaseSchema`, `setErrorHandler`, `reject`, `nothingThere`, the POST/PUT/DELETE handlers, `deleteProjectSchema`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts` (`answer`, `place`, `reportsAbsence`, `reportsUnconfirmed`, `reportsMissingTool`, `reportedProblem`, `deniedIn`, `idOf`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/testlink-client.ts` (`ProjectDeletion`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/tool-caller.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/stdio-tool-caller.ts`

**Mechanism:** Fastify is built with `ajv: {customOptions: {coerceTypes: false}}`, so a wrong-typed field is refused rather than converted; `testCaseSchema` is `required:['name','summary']`, `additionalProperties:false`, and is `satisfies`-checked against `keyof Required<TestCase>` so schema and type cannot drift. `setErrorHandler` turns any `error.validation` into `reply.code(400).send({refusal:'schema', message})` — deliberately carrying no `violations` and no `ruleSetVersion`. Stage two: `findViolations(request.body, bound.testCase)`; non-empty ⇒ `reject()` emits one `request.log.warn({ruleSetVersion, field, rule}, 'Rule violated')` per violation and returns `422` with `versioned({violations})`; nothing is sent to TestLink. Stage three: `McpTestLinkClient.answer(tool, args, alsoTheCallers?)` makes one `tools.call`, and reads failure from three places — `result.isError`, `reportedProblem(content)` (a `{code, message}` where a result should be), and `deniedIn(content)` (`status === false` ⇒ always a throw). `place()` orders the readings: the call's own caller-correctable failure first (`reportsUnconfirmed`, `/Confirmation failed/i`, only passed by `deleteProject`) → `reportsMissingTool` (`/Unknown tool/i`) throws naming `expectedTestLinkMcp` → `reportsAbsence` (`/does not exist|not found/i`) returns the `absent` symbol → everything else throws `TestLink could not be reached through ${tool}`. Routes map `absent` to `nothingThere()` = `404 {message: 'TestLink holds no …'}` (no `refusal`, no violations, no version), `'unconfirmed'` to `409`, success to `201 versioned({id})` for create and `200 versioned({id})` for update, `204` for delete. `idOf` throws when TestLink reports no usable id (`''` and `0` read as none), so a "successful" write with no id never answers 201.

**Why it matters:** Four different non-200s mean four different things to an agent: fix your JSON, fix your prose, fix your id, or stop and escalate. Confusing any two makes the agent loop — the failure this whole shape exists to prevent. It is also where "absence is an answer, everything unrecognised is an outage" is actually implemented; nowhere else decides it.

**Diagram:**
```
POST /projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases  |  PUT /test-cases/:id
  |
 [1] ajv testCaseSchema (required name+summary, additionalProperties
  |   false, coerceTypes false)
  |     fail -> 400 {refusal:'schema', message}   no violations/version
  v
 [2] findViolations(body, bound.testCase)
  |     length>0 -> log.warn per violation
  |             -> 422 {violations[], ruleSetVersion}  NOTHING WRITTEN
  v
 [3] testlink.createTestCase / updateTestCase -> answer() -> place()
        /Confirmation failed/  -> 'unconfirmed' -> 409  (delete project)
        /Unknown tool/         -> throw  (version fault, not TestLink)
        /does not exist|not found/ -> absent -> 404 nothingThere()
        status===false, or unreadable -> throw -> 500
        idOf() finds no id     -> throw -> 500
  v
 201 {id, ruleSetVersion}   |   200 {id, ruleSetVersion}   |   204
```

**Contradicts:**
- `.env.example` (line 11–12) and `README.md` §Running it: `TESTLINK_URL=http://localhost:8090` described as *"the address it publishes on"* with the repo's compose. The default launch in `src/server.ts` is `docker run --rm -i` with **no** `--network host` and no port mapping, so `localhost:8090` inside that container is the container, not the host — the documented default cannot reach the compose TestLink. The repo's own working `.mcp.json` (gitignored) does add `--network host`; `.mcp.json.example` sidesteps it with `https://testlink.example.com`.
- `CONTEXT.md` §Rejection: *"Rejection is the only failure mode."* The write path has four distinct non-success outcomes (400, 422, 404/409, 500), and three of them are explicitly designed not to read as Rejections.

---

### #4 — A read is never refused; the violations ride beside the content

**Key point:** `GET /test-cases/:id` and `GET /reference-documents/:id` run the same Rules over what they serve and answer `200` with the stored content untouched plus a `violations` array beside it — however many fired — so the agent's only window onto existing material shows the fingerprints instead of teaching them on.

**Ground truth:**
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts` (lines 229–241, 399–431)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts` (`listDocuments`, `getDocument`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts` (`getTestCase`, `text`, `first`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql` (`reference_documents`)

**Mechanism:** `getTestCase` reads `read_test_case`, takes `first(held)` (TestLink answers with versions), and projects exactly three fields through `text()` — `name`, `summary`, `preconditions` — so what is served is a `TestCase`, not a TestLink record. The route sends `versioned({testCase, violations: findViolations(testCase, bound.testCase)})`; there is no branch that turns a non-empty `violations` into a refusal. The document route is the mirror: `documents.getDocument(id)` → `select title, body from reference_documents where id = $1` (parameterised, so a caller-supplied id is data), `undefined` ⇒ `404 {message: 'There is no Reference Document …'}` carrying no violations, otherwise `versioned({document, violations: findViolations(document, bound.referenceDocument)})`. `bound.referenceDocument` is a separate `Map` from `bound.testCase`, so a Rule written for one content kind cannot reach the other's fields. `GET /reference-documents` lists `{id, title}` only — bodies are left out. There is no POST/PUT/DELETE for a document anywhere in `app.ts`, and `DocumentStore` declares no write.

**Why it matters:** It is the inversion that makes the project coherent: the same Rules that block a write are advisory on a read, on purpose. A newcomer who symmetrically expects a read to 422 (or expects documents to be writable) will read the missing branches as an oversight rather than as the decision they are.

**Diagram:**
```
 GET /test-cases/:id                GET /reference-documents/:id
        |                                   |
 testlink.getTestCase(id)           documents.getDocument(id)
  read_test_case -> first() ->       select title, body from
  {name, summary, preconditions}     reference_documents where id=$1
        |                                   |
   undefined -> 404                    undefined -> 404
   'TestLink holds no Test Case X'     'There is no Reference Document X'
   (no violations, no version)         (no violations, no version)
        |                                   |
 findViolations(testCase,           findViolations(document,
   bound.testCase)                    bound.referenceDocument)
        |                                   |
        v                                   v
 200 {testCase, violations[],       200 {document, violations[],
      ruleSetVersion}                    ruleSetVersion}

 no 422 on either path; content served exactly as stored
 GET /reference-documents -> [{id, title}]   (no body, no write route)
```

**Contradicts:** none.

---

### #5 — Detection is literal: a Term stands as a word, a Symbol is a character, an Exception suppresses only its own Rule and only where it covers the match

**Key point:** `findViolations` checks every Field against every Rule bound to it in one pass and reports `{field, rule, reason, text, offset}` with no suggested replacement — a Term matched in any casing and only where word characters (`\p{L}\p{N}_-`) do not flank it, a Symbol matched anywhere or only whitespace-flanked, and each Rule's own Exceptions suppressing a hit only when the Exception's span fully contains it.

**Ground truth:**
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts` (whole file)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts` (`TermRule`, `SymbolRule`, `RuleIdentity`, `fieldNames`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql` (`category`, `looks_for`, `flanked`, `rule_exceptions`)
- `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/default-rules.sql`

**Mechanism:** For each `[field, rules]` in the bound `Map`, an absent field value is skipped (so an omitted `preconditions` is not checked). `termViolations` → `spansOf` → `matcherFor(term)`: regex-escape, replace every `\s+` run with `\s+`, flags `giu` — so a phrase matches across a line break and in any casing — then `standsAsWord` requires `isOutsideAWord` on both sides, where a word runs through `-` and `_` (banning `associates` leaves `re-associates` alone; banning `utilise` leaves `utilises` alone). The reported `text` is the casing found, not the casing the Rule was written in. `symbolViolations` walks `value.indexOf(symbol, …)` and, when `rule.flanked === 'whitespace'`, requires `isGap` either side, where the edge of the field counts as whitespace. `suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)` uses the same `spansOf` matcher but with no word-standing test — an Exception matches inside a longer word — and `isSuppressed` requires `offset >= span.start && offset + text.length <= span.end`. Exceptions come only from `rule.exceptions` (populated from `rule_exceptions` rows keyed by `rules.id`), so there is no shared list. The shipped `default-rules.sql` writes 74 Terms and 15 Symbols (verified by count) against all five fields = 89 checks × 5 = 445 enabled Rules, with `on conflict (content_kind, field, rule_id) do nothing` so re-applying cannot switch a tuned-off Rule back on; its trailing comment names what a Term and a Symbol cannot reach (the full "not X, it is Y" frame, the rule of three, thresholds, absence of punctuation, uniform sentence length, Title Case, bold-header bullets).

**Why it matters:** This is the whole of what "validation" means here — there is no model, no scoring, no threshold, and nothing accumulates across requests. Every property the API promises (identical answers for identical input, an explainable rejection, an offset a caller can point at) is a property of these two matchers and nothing else.

**Diagram:**
```
findViolations(content, ruleSets)
  for [field, rules] of ruleSets:      value = content[field]
      value === undefined -> skip this field
      for rule of rules:
        term   -> spansOf(value, rule.term)
                    matcherFor: escape specials, \s+ between words,
                    flags 'giu'  (any casing, any spacing, newlines)
                  -> standsAsWord(prev, next): word char = \p{L}\p{N}_-
                     "utilise" not in "utilises"; "associates" not in
                     "re-associates";  text = the casing FOUND
        symbol -> indexOf loop over value
                    flanked==='whitespace' ? isGap(prev)&&isGap(next)
                    (field edge counts as whitespace) : fires anywhere
        then suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)   <- this Rule only
             isSuppressed: offset >= start && offset+len <= end
             (an Exception matches inside longer words; it covers the
              hit or it does not -- the rest of the field stays under
              the Rule)
  push {field, rule: id, reason, text, offset}   <- no replacement ever
```

**Contradicts:** none. (`README.md`'s "74 terms and 15 symbols", "89 checks", "445 rules" and `docs/adr/0008`'s identical figures were counted against `default-rules.sql` and are correct; the Term/Symbol/Flanking/Exception definitions in `CONTEXT.md` match `violation.ts` line for line, edge-of-field flanking included.)

---
